metaphor_family.caution: Strongly period-flavored; in modern prose it reads as pastiche unless the voice supports it.

metaphor_family.name: root metaphor
metaphor_family.definition: The single underlying comparison from which a whole system of thought or a whole text draws its terms.
metaphor_family.example: A public-works report in which every phrase — burden, load, bearing, failure — treats the county itself as a structure under stress.
metaphor_family.effect: Organizes hundreds of local choices, and quietly decides what questions look sensible.
metaphor_family.caution: A root metaphor you have not identified is a set of assumptions you cannot argue with.

metaphor_family.name: orientational metaphor
metaphor_family.definition: A conceptual metaphor that maps a concept onto spatial orientation — up, down, in, out, front, back.
metaphor_family.example: Morale is up, the budget is down, and the department is behind on everything.
metaphor_family.effect: Makes abstractions feel bodily and immediately intelligible, at the price of smuggling in a value.
metaphor_family.caution: Up is good and down is bad is an argument the sentence never has to make out loud.

metaphor_family.name: ontological metaphor
metaphor_family.definition: Treating an event, activity, or abstraction as a discrete entity or substance with boundaries and behavior.
metaphor_family.example: Corruption entered the agency in the eighties and settled in the permitting office.
metaphor_family.effect: Lets a writer quantify, locate, and blame something that has no physical existence.
metaphor_family.caution: The commonest way an argument acquires an agent it never proved existed.

metaphor_family.name: structural metaphor
metaphor_family.definition: A conceptual metaphor that maps the whole structure of one domain onto another, so its inferences transfer wholesale.
metaphor_family.example: Treating a policy dispute as a war — positions, flanks, casualties, surrender — and then reasoning about it as one.
metaphor_family.effect: Imports a complete logic, including the moves it makes unthinkable.
metaphor_family.register: formal; analysis, criticism, rhetoric of policy
metaphor_family.caution: Its power is exactly its danger: the inferences arrive whether or not they apply.

metaphor_family.name: hypocatastasis
metaphor_family.definition: Implying a comparison by naming the thing only as the figure, without stating both terms as metaphor or simile does.
metaphor_family.example: Get the jackals out of the permitting office.
metaphor_family.effect: Hits harder than metaphor because the comparison is never offered for inspection.
metaphor_family.caution: It smuggles the claim past the reader; in argument, expect to be asked to state it plainly.

metaphor_family.name: negative simile
metaphor_family.definition: A comparison stated by denial: not this familiar thing, but the actual subject.
metaphor_family.example: It was not a crowd that filled the hearing room, and not a jury; it was two hundred people who had lost the same basement.
metaphor_family.effect: Uses the rejected image to supply atmosphere the accepted one lacks.
metaphor_family.register: formal; folk epic, elegy, heightened reportage
metaphor_family.caution: The denied term still colors the sentence, so choose it for what you want smuggled in.

metaphor_family.name: apologue
metaphor_family.definition: A short fictitious narrative, often with animals or objects as actors, told to deliver a moral.
metaphor_family.example: The story of the beaver who dammed the outflow and drowned his own lodge, told at every county meeting for a decade.
metaphor_family.effect: Lets a hard judgment be delivered by a story nobody can take personally.
metaphor_family.register: neutral; didactic writing, oratory, children's forms
metaphor_family.caution: Adult readers resent being taught; the moral works best left unstated.

metaphor_family.name: symbol
metaphor_family.definition: A concrete particular that carries a meaning beyond itself while remaining fully itself in the text.
metaphor_family.example: The rusted gauge stays a rusted gauge and is also everything the county did not want to know.
metaphor_family.effect: Gives a reader a place to keep an abstraction, and lets recurrence do the argument's work.
metaphor_family.caution: A symbol explained is a symbol destroyed; if the prose glosses it, it was an emblem.

metaphor_family.name: anthropopatheia
metaphor_family.definition: Ascribing human passions or bodily parts to God, nature, or an impersonal force.
metaphor_family.example: The river remembered its old channel and went looking for it.
metaphor_family.effect: Gives an indifferent process the shape of an intention, which is what readers can hold in mind.
metaphor_family.register: formal; scripture, elegiac and lyric prose
metaphor_family.caution: In factual writing it is the pathetic fallacy wearing better clothes; it will be read as a claim.

metaphor_family.name: objective correlative
metaphor_family.definition: A set of objects, a situation, or a chain of events chosen to be the formula for a particular emotion, so the emotion arrives without being named.
metaphor_family.example: The kitchen table set for four, the fourth plate turned upside down, the newspaper still folded to the tide chart.
metaphor_family.effect: Produces feeling in the reader instead of reporting it, which is the difference between grief and the word grief.
metaphor_family.register: neutral to formal; fiction, poetry, narrative nonfiction
metaphor_family.caution: Objects chosen for their symbolism rather than their plausibility read as staging.

metonymy_and_naming_family.name: metonymy
metonymy_and_naming_family.definition: Substitution of the name of one thing for that of another closely associated with it.
metonymy_and_naming_family.example: The bench ruled against the plant; the plant appealed to the statehouse.
metonymy_and_naming_family.effect: Names institutions by their instruments, which is compact and quietly attributes agency.
metonymy_and_naming_family.caution: Institutional metonymy hides who decided; in accountability writing, name the person.

metonymy_and_naming_family.name: synecdoche
metonymy_and_naming_family.definition: Substitution of a part for the whole, or a whole for a part.
metonymy_and_naming_family.example: Forty hands walked off the site.
metonymy_and_naming_family.effect: Reduces people or things to the aspect that matters at that moment, for economy or for chill.

metonymy_and_naming_family.name: antonomasia
metonymy_and_naming_family.definition: Substitution of a descriptive epithet or title for a proper name, or of a proper name for a quality.
metonymy_and_naming_family.example: the man from the ministry; a Judas in the accounts department
metonymy_and_naming_family.effect: Names by essence rather than by label, which characterizes as it identifies.

metonymy_and_naming_family.name: vossian antonomasia
metonymy_and_naming_family.definition: Use of a famous proper name as a generic type, typically in the frame the X of Y.
metonymy_and_naming_family.example: the Rasputin of the zoning board
metonymy_and_naming_family.effect: Borrows a whole reputation as shorthand for a character judgment.
metonymy_and_naming_family.caution: Depends entirely on the reader sharing your reference, and dates badly.

metonymy_and_naming_family.name: prosonomasia
metonymy_and_naming_family.definition: Naming a person by a nickname, especially one that comments on them.
metonymy_and_naming_family.example: They called him the Signature, because his was on everything and he had read none of it.
metonymy_and_naming_family.effect: Fixes a judgment in a name the reader will carry through the whole book.
metonymy_and_naming_family.register: informal to neutral; narrative nonfiction, fiction

metonymy_and_naming_family.name: hypocorisma
metonymy_and_naming_family.definition: Use of a diminutive or pet form of a name to soften or belittle.
metonymy_and_naming_family.example: The board never called it a fraud; it was the little problem in receivables.
metonymy_and_naming_family.effect: Shrinks the thing named, either affectionately or as a way of managing it out of sight.

metonymy_and_naming_family.name: metalepsis
metonymy_and_naming_family.definition: Reference to something by means of a figure that is itself figurative, skipping an intermediate step.
metonymy_and_naming_family.example: He had lead in his pencil that quarter, and by spring the whole ledger was writing itself.
metonymy_and_naming_family.effect: Compresses a chain of associations, rewarding the reader who reconstructs the missing links.
metonymy_and_naming_family.caution: The most easily lost figure; if the intermediate link is not common knowledge, the sentence dies.

metonymy_and_naming_family.name: allusion
metonymy_and_naming_family.definition: Indirect reference to a person, event, or text the audience is expected to recognize.
metonymy_and_naming_family.example: The board washed its hands in front of the cameras.
metonymy_and_naming_family.effect: Recruits a whole story in a phrase and flatters the reader who catches it.
metonymy_and_naming_family.caution: An allusion the reader misses is dead weight; an allusion overexplained is worse.

metonymy_and_naming_family.name: epitheton
metonymy_and_naming_family.definition: An adjective or phrase habitually attached to a name to mark its defining quality.
metonymy_and_naming_family.example: the ever-punctual auditor; grey-eyed patience
metonymy_and_naming_family.effect: Fixes a characteristic so firmly that later mentions carry it without repetition.
metonymy_and_naming_family.caution: Stock epithets are the wallpaper of lazy prose; earn each one or drop the adjective.

metonymy_and_naming_family.name: periphrasis
metonymy_and_naming_family.definition: Substitution of a descriptive phrase for a proper name or a plain word.
metonymy_and_naming_family.example: the gentleman whose name is on the letterhead
metonymy_and_naming_family.effect: Elevates, evades, or mocks, depending on why the plain word is being avoided.
metonymy_and_naming_family.caution: The engine of bureaucratic prose; when in doubt, name the thing.

metonymy_and_naming_family.name: euphemism
metonymy_and_naming_family.definition: Substitution of a mild or indirect expression for one thought harsh or blunt.
metonymy_and_naming_family.example: The staff were released to the market.
metonymy_and_naming_family.effect: Softens the blow, and in institutional prose usually softens the accountability with it.
metonymy_and_naming_family.caution: Quote euphemism, do not adopt it; the reader should see whose word it is.

metonymy_and_naming_family.name: dysphemism
metonymy_and_naming_family.definition: Substitution of a deliberately harsh or offensive expression for a neutral one.
metonymy_and_naming_family.example: They did not close the plant; they gutted it and sold the bones.
metonymy_and_naming_family.effect: Forces the reader to feel a violence the neutral term conceals.
metonymy_and_naming_family.caution: Costs credibility in reporting; the facts must be able to carry the heat.

metonymy_and_naming_family.name: ampliatio
metonymy_and_naming_family.definition: Retaining an old name or title for someone or something after it has ceased to apply.
metonymy_and_naming_family.example: The Judge kept the title through twenty years of selling insurance.
metonymy_and_naming_family.effect: Marks how names outlive their warrant, which can be affectionate or damning.

metonymy_and_naming_family.name: pars pro toto
metonymy_and_naming_family.definition: The synecdoche that names a whole by one of its parts.
metonymy_and_naming_family.example: Forty boots on the levee by midnight.
metonymy_and_naming_family.effect: Puts a physical detail where an abstraction would go, and the detail does the counting.
metonymy_and_naming_family.register: neutral; reportage, military and institutional idiom
metonymy_and_naming_family.caution: The chosen part decides what the reader sees; boots and hands make different arguments about the same crew.

metonymy_and_naming_family.name: totum pro parte
metonymy_and_naming_family.definition: The synecdoche that names a part by the whole it belongs to.
metonymy_and_naming_family.example: The county overruled him, meaning three of the five commissioners did.
metonymy_and_naming_family.effect: Lends institutional weight to what may have been one committee on one afternoon.
metonymy_and_naming_family.caution: The standard way responsibility disappears; name the part when the part is the point.

metonymy_and_naming_family.name: eponym
metonymy_and_naming_family.definition: A common noun or adjective formed from a proper name.
metonymy_and_naming_family.example: The whole procedure is a Hollingsworth: file it, wait, and let the season decide.
metonymy_and_naming_family.effect: Compresses a story into a word, and settles a reputation in the process.
metonymy_and_naming_family.register: neutral; technical vocabulary, satire, institutional slang
metonymy_and_naming_family.caution: It fixes a judgment permanently in the language; be sure the person earned it.

metonymy_and_naming_family.name: container for the contained
metonymy_and_naming_family.definition: The metonymy that names what is held by naming what holds it.
metonymy_and_naming_family.example: The hearing room would not hear it.
metonymy_and_naming_family.effect: Gives an abstraction a location and turns a body of people into one actor.
metonymy_and_naming_family.caution: Like all group metonymy, it erases dissent inside the container.

metonymy_and_naming_family.name: author for the work
metonymy_and_naming_family.definition: The metonymy that names a work, style, or body of output by the name of its maker.
metonymy_and_naming_family.example: He had read his Blackstone and not one page of the drainage code.
metonymy_and_naming_family.effect: Signals a whole tradition in one proper noun.
metonymy_and_naming_family.caution: Assumes a reader who knows the name; when they do not, the sentence simply stops.

metonymy_and_naming_family.name: material for the object
metonymy_and_naming_family.definition: The metonymy that names a thing by the substance it is made of.
metonymy_and_naming_family.example: There was more brass at that meeting than at the funeral.
metonymy_and_naming_family.effect: Gives an object a texture and often a class marking that its plain name lacks.
metonymy_and_naming_family.register: neutral; description, period and military idiom

metonymy_and_naming_family.name: place for the institution
metonymy_and_naming_family.definition: The metonymy that names an institution, government, or industry by the place it occupies.
metonymy_and_naming_family.example: Nothing moved until the statehouse decided it should.
metonymy_and_naming_family.effect: Turns a diffuse organization into a single located actor a sentence can hold.
metonymy_and_naming_family.caution: The cheapest way to assign agency without evidence; readers of policy prose have learned to distrust it.

metonymy_and_naming_family.name: charactonym
metonymy_and_naming_family.definition: A name chosen so that its sound or sense declares the bearer's nature or trade.
metonymy_and_naming_family.example: The county engineer in the report is named Mr. Drayton, and he spends nine chapters hauling.
metonymy_and_naming_family.effect: Delivers characterization before a character has done anything.
metonymy_and_naming_family.register: informal to neutral; comedy, satire, allegory
metonymy_and_naming_family.caution: In realist fiction it breaks the frame; in nonfiction, do not remark on a real person's convenient name.

irony_family.name: verbal irony
irony_family.definition: Saying one thing while meaning something markedly different, usually its opposite.
irony_family.example: A masterpiece of scheduling: four inspections, all on the same afternoon.
irony_family.effect: Lets the writer state the false version and let the reader supply the true one.
irony_family.caution: Irony that the reader cannot detect is just a false statement; give it a marker.

irony_family.name: dramatic irony
irony_family.definition: A situation in which the audience knows something a character does not.
irony_family.example: He tells the inspector to come back Thursday, because Thursday is when the crew is off and no one will be there to contradict him. The reader has already seen the Thursday log.
irony_family.effect: Converts every subsequent line into suspense, since the reader watches the gap close.

irony_family.name: situational irony
irony_family.definition: An outcome that inverts what the circumstances led everyone to expect.
irony_family.example: The safety award was announced the week the scaffolding came down.
irony_family.effect: Delivers the judgment through events rather than through the writer's voice.
irony_family.caution: Coincidence is not irony; the inversion has to be of an expectation the text actually built.

irony_family.name: cosmic irony
irony_family.definition: Irony attributed to fate or the order of things, as though a hostile intelligence arranged the outcome.
irony_family.example: The one file he saved from the flood was the one that convicted him.
irony_family.effect: Suggests design behind misfortune, which darkens the whole frame of a narrative.

irony_family.name: structural irony
irony_family.definition: Irony sustained by a work's whole design, usually through a naive narrator whose account the reader corrects continuously.
irony_family.example: A clerk's cheerful memoir of the office that ruined the town, in which every triumph he reports is a disaster the reader can see.
irony_family.effect: Makes reading itself an act of double interpretation from the first page to the last.

irony_family.name: romantic irony
irony_family.definition: A work's self-conscious puncturing of its own illusion, the author stepping visibly through the fiction.
irony_family.example: And here the biographer, who has never seen the town, invites you to picture the town.
irony_family.effect: Reminds the reader that the account is made, which can build trust or dissolve it.

irony_family.name: socratic irony
irony_family.definition: Feigned ignorance or deference adopted in order to draw out and expose another's position.
irony_family.example: I am no engineer, so explain to me how the bolt torqued itself.
irony_family.effect: Lets the questioner disarm resistance and let the opponent do the damage.

irony_family.name: antiphrasis
irony_family.definition: Use of a single word in a sense opposite to its literal one.
irony_family.example: Our benefactor, the landlord.
irony_family.effect: Compresses irony into one word, so the sentence carries no other overhead.

irony_family.name: enantiosis
irony_family.definition: Expressing an idea by explicitly denying its contrary.
irony_family.example: No one would call that a careful inspection.
irony_family.effect: Asserts through negation, which sounds measured while making a strong claim.

irony_family.name: litotes
irony_family.definition: Affirmation expressed by negating the opposite, usually to understate.
irony_family.example: The margins were not insignificant.
irony_family.effect: Understates in a way that reads as restraint and therefore as credibility.
irony_family.caution: Hedged litotes stacked together reads as evasion; the not-un habit is a known style vice.

irony_family.name: meiosis
irony_family.definition: Deliberate belittling of a thing by naming it with a word of lesser magnitude.
irony_family.example: The fire cost them a bit of paperwork and most of the building.
irony_family.effect: Lets the gap between word and fact do the emphasis.

irony_family.name: hyperbole
irony_family.definition: Deliberate exaggeration for emphasis, not intended to be taken literally.
irony_family.example: The form asked for every document the company had produced since the invention of paper.
irony_family.effect: Signals feeling rather than measurement, which is why it persuades and why it is discounted.
irony_family.register: informal to neutral; comic prose, speech
irony_family.caution: In nonfiction, hyperbole next to a real statistic makes the reader doubt the statistic.

irony_family.name: sarcasmus
irony_family.definition: Bitter, cutting irony aimed at wounding its target.
irony_family.example: Congratulations on a spotless record, kept spotless by never being written down.
irony_family.effect: Draws blood and, in the process, tells the reader how much the writer has lost their temper.
irony_family.caution: Costs the appearance of fairness; use sparingly and never against the weaker party.

irony_family.name: mycterismus
irony_family.definition: Mockery delivered obliquely, with a gesture or tone of scorn rather than open attack.
irony_family.example: The chairman, who is of course very busy, sent his regrets and his lawyer.
irony_family.effect: Conveys contempt while maintaining formal courtesy.

irony_family.name: diasyrmus
irony_family.definition: Disparaging an opponent's argument by comparing it to something ridiculous.
irony_family.example: This is a safety plan the way a placemat is a blueprint.
irony_family.effect: Deflates a position by refusing to meet it at its own level of seriousness.
irony_family.caution: Reads as dodging if the argument being ridiculed has not first been stated fairly.

irony_family.name: epitrope
irony_family.definition: Ironically granting permission or conceding a point one expects to be refuted by events.
irony_family.example: Go ahead: publish the maintenance log. Publish all of it.
irony_family.effect: Dares the opponent, wagering that the concession will destroy them.

irony_family.name: accismus
irony_family.definition: Feigned refusal of something one actually desires.
irony_family.example: I could not possibly chair the committee, unless of course no one else will.
irony_family.effect: Lets a character take a thing while appearing to be pressed into it.

irony_family.name: hypocrisis
irony_family.definition: Mocking imitation of an opponent's manner, delivery, or characteristic phrasing.
irony_family.example: Everything, he told us, was under review. Under review. Always under, always review.
irony_family.effect: Turns the opponent's own voice into the evidence against them.
irony_family.caution: Slides into caricature quickly; quote before you imitate.

irony_family.name: stable irony
irony_family.definition: Irony whose real meaning the reader is meant to reconstruct with confidence and then stand on.
irony_family.example: Of course the file was complete. The county had said so in writing, twice, and the second time in bold.
irony_family.effect: Builds a coalition between writer and reader against the stated surface.
irony_family.caution: Requires shared ground; a reader who does not already agree hears only the surface.

irony_family.name: unstable irony
irony_family.definition: Irony that undercuts the stated meaning without offering any secure position to move to, including the ironist's own.
irony_family.example: The narrator explains why nobody could have known, then explains why he in particular could not have known, then stops explaining.
irony_family.effect: Leaves the reader without footing, which is the point when the subject has none either.
irony_family.register: formal; modernist and postmodern fiction, self-implicating essay
irony_family.caution: Easily read as evasion or as a writer who could not decide.

irony_family.name: parody
irony_family.definition: Close imitation of a specific work, author, or style whose exaggeration exposes its mannerisms.
irony_family.example: A drainage report written in the cadence of scripture, complete with a genealogy of culverts.
irony_family.effect: Criticizes a style from inside it, which is harder to rebut than criticizing it from outside.
irony_family.register: informal to formal; satire, criticism, comic set piece
irony_family.caution: Dies with its target; parody of a style the reader does not know is only bad writing.

irony_family.name: travesty
irony_family.definition: Treating a dignified subject in a deliberately low or vulgar style.
irony_family.example: The founding of the waterworks retold in the vocabulary of a bar fight.
irony_family.effect: Strips ceremony off an institution by refusing it the register it expects.
irony_family.caution: Contempt is easier than argument, and readers can tell which one they are getting.

irony_family.name: burlesque
irony_family.definition: Comic incongruity between a subject and the style used for it, in either direction.
irony_family.example: A eulogy for a broken pump, delivered in full.
irony_family.effect: Makes the mismatch itself the joke, so the target need never be named.
irony_family.caution: Sustained burlesque exhausts a reader faster than any other comic mode.

irony_family.name: mock-heroic
irony_family.definition: Applying the machinery of epic — invocations, catalogues, similes, grand diction — to a trivial subject.
irony_family.example: Sing, muse, of the parking dispute that consumed the March meeting and three careers.
irony_family.effect: Measures the subject against the form and lets the gap do the mockery.
irony_family.caution: The joke is legible for about a page; beyond that it needs a real plot underneath.

irony_family.name: paradoxical encomium
irony_family.definition: Formal praise of something normally held worthless, shameful, or absurd.
irony_family.example: In praise of the unanswered letter, which has never yet been proved wrong.
irony_family.effect: Tests the machinery of praise by running it on a subject that ought to break it.
irony_family.caution: Only works if the praise is genuinely well made; a sloppy encomium is just a joke about a bad thing.

irony_family.name: horatian satire
irony_family.definition: Satire in a tolerant, urbane register that laughs at folly rather than denouncing vice.
irony_family.example: A wry chapter on the county's habit of numbering its committees, written by someone who has served on four.
irony_family.effect: Keeps the audience inside the joke, including the part of the audience being satirized.
irony_family.caution: Genial satire changes nothing, which is sometimes exactly what its target is counting on.

irony_family.name: juvenalian satire
irony_family.definition: Satire in a bitter, indignant register that attacks vice and corruption with contempt rather than amusement.
irony_family.example: A chapter that names the three men who signed the waiver and does not make a single joke.
irony_family.effect: Converts anger into structure; the reader is asked to be outraged, not entertained.
irony_family.caution: Sustained scorn exhausts credit fast; without evidence underneath it reads as temper.

definition_and_division_figures.name: definitio
definition_and_division_figures.definition: Explicit statement of what a term means for the purposes of the argument.
definition_and_division_figures.example: By deferred maintenance I mean work that was scheduled, funded, and then not done.
definition_and_division_figures.effect: Fixes the ground of the dispute before the dispute begins.

definition_and_division_figures.name: horismus
definition_and_division_figures.definition: Definition by sharp contrast with a near neighbor, saying what a thing is by saying what it is not.
definition_and_division_figures.example: This was not negligence, which forgets; it was policy, which decides.
definition_and_division_figures.effect: Separates two things the reader had been treating as one.
definition_and_division_figures.caution: The not-X-but-Y frame again; one per section, and only where the confusion is real.

definition_and_division_figures.name: anthorismus
definition_and_division_figures.definition: Counter-definition: replacing an opponent's definition of a term with a contrary one.
definition_and_division_figures.example: They call it a settlement. A settlement is what you reach with someone who can still sue you.
definition_and_division_figures.effect: Reclaims the vocabulary of the dispute, which often decides the dispute.

definition_and_division_figures.name: aphorismus
definition_and_division_figures.definition: Calling into question whether a word is rightly applied to a thing.
definition_and_division_figures.example: Consultation? Six people in a room who were told the answer beforehand?
definition_and_division_figures.effect: Attacks the label rather than the fact, forcing the opponent to defend their vocabulary.

definition_and_division_figures.name: distinctio
definition_and_division_figures.definition: Explicitly drawing out the several senses of an ambiguous word to prevent confusion.
definition_and_division_figures.example: Approved can mean signed, or reviewed, or merely received; here it means received.
definition_and_division_figures.effect: Closes off the escape routes an equivocal word offers an opponent.

definition_and_division_figures.name: paradiastole
definition_and_division_figures.definition: Redescribing a vice as an adjacent virtue, or a virtue as a vice.
definition_and_division_figures.example: He is not evasive; he is careful. She is not thorough; she is obstructive.
definition_and_division_figures.effect: Shows how the same conduct is renamed depending on who is describing it.

definition_and_division_figures.name: partitio
definition_and_division_figures.definition: Dividing a subject into its constituent parts and announcing that the treatment will follow them.
definition_and_division_figures.example: Three things failed: the design, the inspection, and the response. Take them in order.
definition_and_division_figures.effect: Gives the reader a map, which buys patience for a long treatment.

definition_and_division_figures.name: merismus
definition_and_division_figures.definition: Naming a whole by listing its complementary parts or extremes.
definition_and_division_figures.example: Neither the day crew nor the night crew, neither the office nor the site, had ever seen the drawing.
definition_and_division_figures.effect: Asserts totality by exhausting the alternatives rather than claiming it outright.

definition_and_division_figures.name: diaeresis
definition_and_division_figures.definition: Division of a genus into its species in order to treat them separately.
definition_and_division_figures.example: Failures of this kind are of three species: unfunded, unassigned, and unrecorded.
definition_and_division_figures.effect: Converts a vague category into a set of handles the argument can grip.

definition_and_division_figures.name: dialysis
definition_and_division_figures.definition: Setting out alternatives so that each, taken separately, supports the same conclusion.
definition_and_division_figures.example: Either they knew, which is fraud, or they did not, which is incompetence at a scale no license survives.
definition_and_division_figures.effect: Traps the opponent between two doors that open on the same room.
definition_and_division_figures.caution: Only sound if the alternatives are genuinely exhaustive; otherwise it is a false dilemma.

definition_and_division_figures.name: enumeratio
definition_and_division_figures.definition: Detailing the parts, causes, or consequences of a thing, usually as a numbered or listed series.
definition_and_division_figures.example: The consequences were four: a fine, a suspension, a lost contract, and a town without a clinic.
definition_and_division_figures.effect: Makes an abstraction countable, which reads as rigor.

definition_and_division_figures.name: distributio
definition_and_division_figures.definition: Assigning each part of a divided subject to its proper agent or treatment.
definition_and_division_figures.example: The engineer owns the design, the county owns the inspection, and the owner owns the decision to proceed anyway.
definition_and_division_figures.effect: Distributes responsibility explicitly, which is the groundwork of any accountability argument.

definition_and_division_figures.name: prosapodosis
definition_and_division_figures.definition: Supplying a reason for each of the divided parts immediately after naming them.
definition_and_division_figures.example: The permit lapsed, because no one renewed it; the crew stayed, because no one told them; the wall fell, because the crew stayed.
definition_and_division_figures.effect: Fuses division and justification so the structure carries the proof.

definition_and_division_figures.name: eutrepismus
definition_and_division_figures.definition: Numbering and ordering the parts under discussion.
definition_and_division_figures.example: First, the money was moved. Second, the minutes were revised. Third, the auditor was replaced.
definition_and_division_figures.effect: Imposes sequence and finality; the reader accepts a numbered list as complete.
definition_and_division_figures.caution: Numbered lists in narrative prose read as slide decks; keep them where the order matters.

definition_and_division_figures.name: expeditio
definition_and_division_figures.definition: Listing all the possibilities and then eliminating all but one.
definition_and_division_figures.example: The leak came from the roof, the pipe, or the tank. The roof was new; the pipe was dry. That leaves the tank.
definition_and_division_figures.effect: Simulates a proof by exhaustion and leaves the survivor looking demonstrated.
definition_and_division_figures.caution: Its persuasive force depends entirely on the list being complete; readers will test that.

definition_and_division_figures.name: systrophe
definition_and_division_figures.definition: Heaping up descriptions and attributes of a subject without giving its name.
definition_and_division_figures.example: The thing that eats the budget in silence, that no minute records, that every department blames on another: call it what you like.
definition_and_division_figures.effect: Builds the subject out of its properties so the reader names it themselves.

definition_and_division_figures.name: taxis
definition_and_division_figures.definition: Assigning to each thing named its proper attribute, office, or share, so a subject is divided by what belongs to each part.
definition_and_division_figures.example: To the state, the standard; to the county, the inspection; to the contractor, the concrete; to the school, the water.
definition_and_division_figures.effect: Distributes responsibility visibly, which makes the missing assignment conspicuous.
definition_and_division_figures.register: formal; legal and administrative prose, argument

definition_and_division_figures.name: etymologia
definition_and_division_figures.definition: Arguing from or defining by the origin and derivation of a word.
definition_and_division_figures.example: A variance is a difference, and the file records forty years of differences from a rule nobody was willing to repeal.
definition_and_division_figures.effect: Gives a definition the appearance of having been there before the dispute.
definition_and_division_figures.caution: A word's history is not its meaning; the etymological fallacy lives here.

definition_and_division_figures.name: ostensive definition
definition_and_division_figures.definition: Fixing a term's meaning by pointing to instances of it rather than by stating its properties.
definition_and_division_figures.example: Deferred maintenance looks like this: that gauge, that culvert, that roof.
definition_and_division_figures.effect: Makes an abstraction inspectable, and lets the reader generalize instead of being told.
definition_and_division_figures.caution: Examples always carry more than the term; readers will import the incidental features too.

definition_and_division_figures.name: stipulative definition
definition_and_division_figures.definition: Announcing the sense in which a term will be used in this text, without claiming it is the ordinary sense.
definition_and_division_figures.example: By failure I mean, throughout, any event the design was supposed to survive and did not.
definition_and_division_figures.effect: Buys precision cheaply and forecloses a whole class of objections.
definition_and_division_figures.register: formal; scholarship, technical and legal writing
definition_and_division_figures.caution: A stipulation cannot settle a question that turns on the ordinary sense of the word.

definition_and_division_figures.name: persuasive definition
definition_and_division_figures.definition: Redefining a term so that its favorable or unfavorable charge is transferred to a new referent.
definition_and_division_figures.example: Real accountability, properly understood, means letting the people who did the work write the report.
definition_and_division_figures.effect: Wins the argument at the definition stage, before any evidence is offered.
definition_and_division_figures.caution: Recognizable and resented; readers who spot it discount everything that follows.

definition_and_division_figures.name: operational definition
definition_and_division_figures.definition: Defining a term by the procedure used to measure or detect the thing.
definition_and_division_figures.example: For this report, flooded means water standing above the door sill for more than one hour.
definition_and_division_figures.effect: Makes a claim checkable and moves the dispute onto the procedure, where it can be settled.
definition_and_division_figures.register: formal; scientific, technical, and policy writing
definition_and_division_figures.caution: The measure quietly becomes the concept; what the procedure cannot see stops existing.

definition_and_division_figures.name: apophatic definition
definition_and_division_figures.definition: Defining something by stating what it is not, in a series that narrows the field without ever naming the thing.
definition_and_division_figures.example: It was not sabotage, not a hundred-year storm, and not a design nobody could have checked.
definition_and_division_figures.effect: Clears the ground and leaves the reader to supply the remaining term, which they then own.
definition_and_division_figures.caution: A negative series that never closes is evasion; readers keep count of what you have ruled out.

definition_and_division_figures.name: definition by genus and differentia
definition_and_division_figures.definition: The classical form of definition: name the class the thing belongs to, then the feature that distinguishes it within that class.
definition_and_division_figures.example: A variance is a permit — that is the genus — issued in spite of the rule rather than under it.
definition_and_division_figures.effect: Gives a definition that can be tested for both over- and under-inclusion.
definition_and_division_figures.caution: Only as good as the genus; a badly chosen class hides the real dispute one level up.

question_and_address_figures.name: erotema
question_and_address_figures.definition: A question asked for effect, whose answer is presumed and not supplied.
question_and_address_figures.example: How many inspections does a bridge need before the first one happens?
question_and_address_figures.effect: Recruits the reader into supplying the conclusion, which feels like their own.
question_and_address_figures.caution: The most conspicuous filler in generated prose; a paragraph that opens on a question and answers it in the next line is a tell.

question_and_address_figures.name: hypophora
question_and_address_figures.definition: Raising a question and immediately answering it oneself.
question_and_address_figures.example: Who authorized the change? The same office that later ordered the file destroyed.
question_and_address_figures.effect: Controls the reader's questions by asking them first and answering on your own terms.
question_and_address_figures.caution: Overused it turns exposition into a catechism; alternate with plain declarative structure.

question_and_address_figures.name: percontatio
question_and_address_figures.definition: An open question that invites reflection rather than a determinate answer.
question_and_address_figures.example: What does a town owe a company that built it and then left?
question_and_address_figures.effect: Opens a space the essay will occupy, without pretending the answer is already settled.

question_and_address_figures.name: pysma
question_and_address_figures.definition: Asking several questions in succession, each requiring a different and complex answer.
question_and_address_figures.example: Who signed it? On whose authority? With what inspection? And why in a week when the office was closed?
question_and_address_figures.effect: Overwhelms by accumulation; the unanswered pile becomes the accusation.
question_and_address_figures.caution: Four questions with no answers reads as bluster unless the text supplies them soon after.

question_and_address_figures.name: epiplexis
question_and_address_figures.definition: Asking questions in order to reproach or shame rather than to elicit information.
question_and_address_figures.example: Did you imagine the wall would hold because the paperwork did?
question_and_address_figures.effect: Turns interrogation into rebuke, and the target into a defendant.

question_and_address_figures.name: aporia
question_and_address_figures.definition: Expression of real or feigned doubt about how to proceed or what to think.
question_and_address_figures.example: I do not know what to call a system that fails this reliably. Design seems too generous; accident, too kind.
question_and_address_figures.effect: Shows the writer thinking, which builds trust before the conclusion arrives.
question_and_address_figures.caution: Feigned doubt is transparent to a hostile reader; do not perform uncertainty you have already resolved.

question_and_address_figures.name: anacoenosis
question_and_address_figures.definition: Asking the audience or even the opponent for their opinion or judgment on the matter.
question_and_address_figures.example: Put yourself at that desk with that memo in front of you. What do you sign?
question_and_address_figures.effect: Makes the reader a participant, which commits them to the answer they give themselves.

question_and_address_figures.name: comprobatio
question_and_address_figures.definition: Complimenting the audience or the judges in order to secure their goodwill.
question_and_address_figures.example: You have read the appendix, which is more than the committee that commissioned it did.
question_and_address_figures.effect: Flatters while establishing the standard the reader is now expected to uphold.
question_and_address_figures.caution: Obvious flattery reads as manipulation; keep it specific and small.

question_and_address_figures.name: ratiocinatio
question_and_address_figures.definition: Reasoning aloud by putting questions to oneself and answering them.
question_and_address_figures.example: Why did I keep the receipts? Because I had been told twice that the account was closed, and the account kept paying.
question_and_address_figures.effect: Exposes the writer's reasoning chain, which reads as candor and invites agreement step by step.

question_and_address_figures.name: apostrophe
question_and_address_figures.definition: Turning from the audience to address directly an absent person, an abstraction, or an object.
question_and_address_figures.example: And you, the town that voted twice for the bond, where were you at the hearing?
question_and_address_figures.effect: Breaks the frame of address, raising the emotional pitch sharply.
question_and_address_figures.caution: The purple end of the register; one apostrophe in a book, and only at a genuine peak.

question_and_address_figures.name: prosopopoeia
question_and_address_figures.definition: Putting speech into the mouth of an absent, dead, or imaginary person, or of an abstraction.
question_and_address_figures.example: If the building could speak, it would say only that it was patched, never repaired.
question_and_address_figures.effect: Introduces a witness who cannot be cross-examined but whom the reader wants to believe.
question_and_address_figures.caution: Invented testimony in factual writing must be unmistakably marked as a figure.

question_and_address_figures.name: sermocinatio
question_and_address_figures.definition: Attributing invented but characteristic speech to a real person to reveal their character.
question_and_address_figures.example: He would say, and everyone in the office could recite it, that a signature is only a date with a name on it.
question_and_address_figures.effect: Characterizes through voice rather than description.
question_and_address_figures.caution: In nonfiction, invented dialogue needs a signal; readers assume quotation marks mean a record.

question_and_address_figures.name: ethopoeia
question_and_address_figures.definition: Imitating another's character, manner, or way of thinking in order to present them from the inside.
question_and_address_figures.example: Consider it from the inspector's side: forty sites, one truck, a supervisor who counts visits and not findings.
question_and_address_figures.effect: Builds understanding or indictment by inhabiting the other position.

question_and_address_figures.name: dialogismus
question_and_address_figures.definition: Speaking in the imagined voice of another person or party within one's own discourse.
question_and_address_figures.example: The company's answer is familiar: we followed the code, the code was the standard, the standard was the law.
question_and_address_figures.effect: Stages the opposition's case in its own idiom before dismantling it.

question_and_address_figures.name: invocatio
question_and_address_figures.definition: A formal call upon a deity, muse, or authority for aid or witness at the outset of a work.
question_and_address_figures.example: Whatever keeps records when the archives burn, help me get this order right.
question_and_address_figures.effect: Marks the beginning as ceremonial and stakes the work on something larger than the writer.
question_and_address_figures.caution: In modern prose it survives mainly as pastiche or joke.

question_and_address_figures.name: obtestatio
question_and_address_figures.definition: Calling on a person, a deity, or the audience as witness, often with entreaty.
question_and_address_figures.example: I call the surviving crew to witness what the schedule said that week.
question_and_address_figures.effect: Puts the writer's credibility on the line in front of named witnesses.

question_and_address_figures.name: parrhesia
question_and_address_figures.definition: Candid speech that risks offending the audience, often with an acknowledgment of the risk.
question_and_address_figures.example: I will say the thing the funders will not enjoy: the pilot worked because it was small, and it will not scale.
question_and_address_figures.effect: Buys credibility by demonstrating willingness to pay a price for the truth.
question_and_address_figures.caution: Performed bluntness is a well-known move; if there is no real risk, the figure is empty.

question_and_address_figures.name: eidolopoeia
question_and_address_figures.definition: Presenting a dead person as speaking, in their own voice.
question_and_address_figures.example: Ask the man who signed it. He would say what he said in 1974: the money was not there and the rule did not say must.
question_and_address_figures.effect: Brings a witness into the room who cannot be cross-examined, which is both its power and its problem.
question_and_address_figures.caution: In nonfiction, invented speech for a real dead person is a fabrication however clearly it is framed.

question_and_address_figures.name: captatio benevolentiae
question_and_address_figures.definition: An opening move that solicits the audience's goodwill by professing modesty, shared ground, or respect for their judgment.
question_and_address_figures.example: You have lived with this river longer than I have studied it, and I expect to be corrected on at least three things.
question_and_address_figures.effect: Buys a hearing from an audience with reason to resist.
question_and_address_figures.caution: Modesty that runs past two sentences reads as either fishing or fear.

question_and_address_figures.name: breaking the fourth wall
question_and_address_figures.definition: Direct acknowledgement of the audience or of the work's own status as a made thing, from inside the work.
question_and_address_figures.example: I am about to describe the meeting, and you should know that I have three accounts of it that do not agree.
question_and_address_figures.effect: Converts a reader from an observer into an addressee, and puts the writer's method on the table.
question_and_address_figures.register: informal to neutral; metafiction, essay, documentary narration
question_and_address_figures.caution: Each break costs immersion; in fiction, spend it only where the gain is structural.

question_and_address_figures.name: aside
question_and_address_figures.definition: A remark delivered past the ostensible addressee, meant for the audience or the reader alone.
question_and_address_figures.example: He assured the room the study was under way. (It was not. It had been under way for six years.)
question_and_address_figures.effect: Opens a second channel in which the writer can say what the scene cannot.
question_and_address_figures.register: informal to neutral; drama, comic narration, essay
question_and_address_figures.caution: The aside must know something the scene cannot show; otherwise it is only the writer editorializing.

question_and_address_figures.name: soliloquy
question_and_address_figures.definition: Extended speech in which a character alone gives their thought directly to the audience.
question_and_address_figures.example: Alone in the records room, he counts the reasons it was not his to fix, and gets to four.
question_and_address_figures.effect: Puts interior reasoning on the outside where it can be judged as an argument.
question_and_address_figures.register: formal; drama, dramatic monologue, first-person fiction
question_and_address_figures.caution: Prose has cheaper access to interiority; a soliloquy in a novel needs a reason to be a performance.

question_and_address_figures.name: leading question
question_and_address_figures.definition: A question framed so that it supplies its own answer or presupposes a contested fact.
question_and_address_figures.example: When did the office decide the gauge was not worth repairing?
question_and_address_figures.effect: Advances a claim in the grammatical clothes of an inquiry.
question_and_address_figures.caution: In writing it is a fallacy with a question mark; a reader who spots the presupposition stops trusting the questioner.

question_and_address_figures.name: maieutic questioning
question_and_address_figures.definition: A sequence of questions designed to draw a conclusion out of the respondent rather than to refute them.
question_and_address_figures.example: What is the culvert sized for? And what fell in June? And what would you have had to believe to call that sizing adequate?
question_and_address_figures.effect: Lets the reader arrive at the conclusion themselves, which makes it very hard to give up.
question_and_address_figures.caution: Readers resent being walked; if the answer is obvious three questions out, state it.

description_figures.name: enargeia
description_figures.definition: Description so vivid that the scene seems present before the audience's eyes.
description_figures.example: Rebar sticking out of the slab like wet hair; the smell of cut concrete; a hard hat upside down in the standing water.
description_figures.effect: Converts report into witness, which is the strongest persuasive resource description has.
description_figures.caution: Requires concrete particulars; adjectives alone produce atmosphere, not presence.

description_figures.name: energeia
description_figures.definition: Vigor of expression that makes a description feel active and in motion rather than merely visible.
description_figures.example: The crane swung, checked, swung again, and the load walked itself out over the street.
description_figures.effect: Puts the reader inside the event's momentum rather than in front of its picture.

description_figures.name: diaskeue
description_figures.definition: Vivid description whose purpose is to arouse the audience's emotion rather than to inform.
description_figures.example: Three shifts of men who had asked, in writing, twice, for a second ladder.
description_figures.effect: Selects and amplifies the details that will move, and omits the ones that will not.
description_figures.caution: This is where description becomes advocacy; keep the facts intact even when the framing is warm.

description_figures.name: ekphrasis
description_figures.definition: Extended verbal description of a work of visual art or a made object.
description_figures.example: The commemorative plaque lists forty names in two columns, the second column set slightly lower, as though added after the plate was cast.
description_figures.effect: Makes an object argue by holding the reader inside its details.

description_figures.name: blazon
description_figures.definition: A poetic catalogue itemizing, part by part, the features of a person, usually in praise.
description_figures.example: Her hands, ink at the knuckle; her collar, pressed; her patience, older than the building.
description_figures.effect: Praises by inventory, which can idealize or, held too long, dismember.
description_figures.caution: The convention is exhausted and, applied to women's bodies, freighted; invert it or leave it alone.

description_figures.name: effictio
description_figures.definition: Orderly head-to-toe description of a person's outward appearance.
description_figures.example: Grey at the temples, heavy through the shoulders, a limp on the left, and shoes that had been resoled twice.
description_figures.effect: Delivers a whole physical impression in a fixed sequence the reader can hold.
description_figures.register: neutral; fiction, forensic and journalistic description
description_figures.caution: The full head-to-toe read is slow; most modern prose takes three details and moves.

description_figures.name: prosopographia
description_figures.definition: Vivid description of a person's appearance and bearing so as to make them present.
description_figures.example: He stood the way men stand when they expect to be asked to leave.
description_figures.effect: Renders character through carriage rather than catalogue.

description_figures.name: characterismus
description_figures.definition: Description of a person's body and mind together, joining outward marks to inward traits.
description_figures.example: A careful man, careful with his coat and his commitments, who had never once been early for anything he did not want.
description_figures.effect: Closes the gap between what a person looks like and what they are.

description_figures.name: notatio
description_figures.definition: Description of a person's character by the signs and habits that reveal it.
description_figures.example: He kept two calendars: one for what he had agreed to and one for what he intended to do.
description_figures.effect: Proves character by evidence instead of asserting it with adjectives.

description_figures.name: icon
description_figures.definition: Portraying a person or thing by the image of something else it resembles.
description_figures.example: The agency in those years was a lighthouse with the lamp removed: the tower kept, the function gone.
description_figures.effect: Gives the reader a picture to hold in place of an abstraction.

description_figures.name: mimesis
description_figures.definition: Imitation of another's gestures, pronunciation, or manner in the course of describing them.
description_figures.example: He would spread his hands, palms up, the way he did when a number would not sit still.
description_figures.effect: Reproduces a person as motion, which is more memorable than any list of traits.

description_figures.name: peristasis
description_figures.definition: Description of the attendant circumstances of an event, person, or place.
description_figures.example: It was the last week of the fiscal year, the office was half-staffed for the holiday, and the fax machine had been unplugged since Tuesday.
description_figures.effect: Establishes the conditions that make an action intelligible or inexcusable.

description_figures.name: topographia
description_figures.definition: Vivid description of an actual place.
description_figures.example: The plant sits below the road, so that everyone who drives to work looks down into its yard.
description_figures.effect: Fixes the ground of the story and lets geography carry meaning.

description_figures.name: topothesia
description_figures.definition: Description of an imaginary or non-existent place.
description_figures.example: Imagine a county where every permit is public on the day it is issued.
description_figures.effect: Uses an invented place as a standard against which the real one is measured.

description_figures.name: chronographia
description_figures.definition: Vivid description of a time, season, or period.
description_figures.example: That was the autumn when everyone was waiting for the audit and nobody would repaint anything.
description_figures.effect: Gives a stretch of time a texture, so the reader feels duration rather than dates.

description_figures.name: pragmatographia
description_figures.definition: Vivid description of an action or event as it unfolds.
description_figures.example: The crew set the last panel at four, tightened four of the eight bolts, and went to the truck for the torque wrench that was not there.
description_figures.effect: Reconstructs an event in sequence so the reader can locate the point of failure.

description_figures.name: geographia
description_figures.definition: Description of the earth, a region, or a territory at scale.
description_figures.example: The watershed runs from the ridge to the state line, and everything on it drains past three towns and one landfill.
description_figures.effect: Sets a local story inside the physical system that produced it.

description_figures.name: anemographia
description_figures.definition: Description of the wind, and by extension of weather as an active force.
description_figures.example: The wind came down the valley all afternoon in long pushes that made the tarpaulins boom like sails.
description_figures.effect: Gives an invisible force a body, usually to raise tension in a scene.
description_figures.caution: Weather description is where drafts go slack; keep it doing narrative work.

description_figures.name: astrothesia
description_figures.definition: Description of the stars or the night sky.
description_figures.example: By two in the morning the water had stopped rising and the sky over the fairground was the hard, particular black that follows a cleared storm.
description_figures.effect: Supplies scale and indifference; the sky is the cheapest available measure of how small the event is.
description_figures.register: formal; epic, lyric description, nature writing
description_figures.caution: The most reached-for consolation image in the language; earn it or cut it.

description_figures.name: chorographia
description_figures.definition: Description of a region, province, or nation as a whole.
description_figures.example: It is a county of shallow soil over rock, where every road follows a watercourse because nothing else was ever level enough.
description_figures.effect: Establishes the terms a whole book will argue in, before a single person appears.
description_figures.register: formal; history, travel writing, regional nonfiction
description_figures.caution: Regional description slides into regional character; keep the claim on the land.

description_figures.name: dendrographia
description_figures.definition: Description of trees or of a wooded place.
description_figures.example: The sycamores along the old channel still lean where the water pushed them, sixty years after the water moved.
description_figures.effect: Puts a slow clock in the scene; trees hold a record no document does.

description_figures.name: hydrographia
description_figures.definition: Description of water — a river, a sea, a flood, or a body of standing water.
description_figures.example: It came across the field in a sheet, not a wave, and it was the color of the field.
description_figures.effect: Gives a formless force a shape the reader can hold, which is most of the work in flood writing.
description_figures.caution: Water attracts every cliche in the language; describe this water, at this hour.

description_figures.name: counterblazon
description_figures.definition: The inverted blazon: an itemized description that catalogues a subject's defects part by part.
description_figures.example: Cracked apron, silted invert, headwall out of plumb, and a grate somebody had cut with a torch.
description_figures.effect: Uses the form of praise to deliver an indictment, item by item.
description_figures.register: neutral; satire, inspection and forensic writing
description_figures.caution: Applied to a person it is cruelty with a formal excuse; applied to a thing it is a survey.

description_figures.name: defamiliarization
description_figures.definition: Describing a familiar thing as if seen for the first time, so that habit is stripped off it.
description_figures.example: A culvert is a hole the county maintains on purpose, and everything above it depends on the hole staying a hole.
description_figures.effect: Restores attention to what the reader had stopped seeing, which is often the whole point of the chapter.
description_figures.register: neutral to formal; literary fiction, essay, criticism
description_figures.caution: Strangeness for its own sake reads as whimsy; the estrangement has to reveal something.

description_figures.name: thick description
description_figures.definition: Description that reports not only what was done but the layers of meaning and context that make the act legible to its participants.
description_figures.example: He signed on the second line rather than the first, which in that office meant he had read it and would not defend it.
description_figures.effect: Turns observed behavior into evidence about a culture rather than an anecdote.
description_figures.caution: The layers are the writer's interpretation; say how you know what the gesture meant.

description_figures.name: significant detail
description_figures.definition: One selected particular chosen to carry the weight of a whole scene, character, or condition.
description_figures.example: There was a calendar in the pump house still turned to the month of the flood.
description_figures.effect: Achieves in one clause what a paragraph of general description cannot, because the reader does the generalizing.
description_figures.caution: Only significant if it is not also decorative; two telling details in a row cancel each other.

description_figures.name: locus amoenus
description_figures.definition: The topos of the idealized pleasant place — shade, water, grass, birdsong — set apart from the world's business.
description_figures.example: Before the impoundment there was a bend with willows and a gravel bar, and every family in the township had a photograph taken on it.
description_figures.effect: Establishes a standard of the good that the rest of the narrative can violate.
description_figures.caution: Two thousand years old and it shows; the details must be local or the passage is wallpaper.

description_figures.name: locus horridus
description_figures.definition: The counter-topos of the horrid place — the blasted, fouled, or unquiet landscape that mirrors disorder.
description_figures.example: What is there now is a flat of dried silt, a standpipe, and the smell that comes off ground that has been wet too long.
description_figures.effect: Puts moral disorder into terrain, so the reader arrives at the judgment through the senses.
description_figures.caution: One step from the pathetic fallacy; keep the landscape doing landscape things.

argumentation_figures.name: prolepsis
argumentation_figures.definition: Rhetorical sense: anticipating an objection and answering it before the opponent can raise it. Distinct from the narratological prolepsis, which is the flash-forward.
argumentation_figures.example: It will be said that the code did not require a second inspection. It did not. It also did not forbid one, and the budget line for it was spent.
argumentation_figures.effect: Removes the opponent's best move and makes the writer look candid for having named it.
argumentation_figures.caution: Raising a weak version of the objection is the commonest cheat; steelman or skip it.

argumentation_figures.name: concessio
argumentation_figures.definition: Granting a point to the opponent, usually in order to gain a stronger position on the point that matters.
argumentation_figures.example: Grant every word of the schedule defense. The bolt was still never torqued.
argumentation_figures.effect: Buys credibility cheaply and narrows the dispute to the ground you have chosen.

argumentation_figures.name: paralipsis
argumentation_figures.definition: Emphasizing something by conspicuously declining to mention it.
argumentation_figures.example: I will not dwell on the three prior citations, or on who signed them.
argumentation_figures.effect: Delivers the charge while claiming the restraint of having withheld it.
argumentation_figures.caution: Transparent and widely disliked; readers who catch it discount everything around it.

argumentation_figures.name: antanagoge
argumentation_figures.definition: Balancing an unfavorable admission with a favorable point, so the two are weighed together.
argumentation_figures.example: The pilot ran over budget, but it produced the only inspection data the county has ever had.
argumentation_figures.effect: Prevents a concession from becoming a defeat.

argumentation_figures.name: apodioxis
argumentation_figures.definition: Rejecting an argument outright as absurd, irrelevant, or beneath reply.
argumentation_figures.example: That the rain caused it is not a theory; it is an alibi with a weather report attached.
argumentation_figures.effect: Refuses to legitimize a position by arguing with it.
argumentation_figures.caution: Only safe when the reader already sees the absurdity; otherwise it reads as dodging.

argumentation_figures.name: antirrhesis
argumentation_figures.definition: Rejecting an opponent's argument by attacking the authority or worthlessness of its source.
argumentation_figures.example: The certification comes from a body funded by the firms it certifies and staffed by their retirees.
argumentation_figures.effect: Removes the ground under an argument rather than contesting its content.
argumentation_figures.caution: One step from ad hominem; the attack must go to reliability, not to character at large.

argumentation_figures.name: metastasis
argumentation_figures.definition: Turning an opponent's charge back upon them.
argumentation_figures.example: They accuse the inspectors of delay. The inspectors waited eleven months for a drawing the company had already printed.
argumentation_figures.effect: Converts a defense into an offense in a single move.

argumentation_figures.name: anticategoria
argumentation_figures.definition: Meeting an accusation with a counter-accusation of the same kind.
argumentation_figures.example: The county says the firm kept no records. The firm's reply is that the county lost the ones it was sent.
argumentation_figures.effect: Muddies fault by making the charge mutual.
argumentation_figures.caution: As an argument it is a fallacy; report it as a move rather than making it.

argumentation_figures.name: inter se pugnantia
argumentation_figures.definition: Reproaching an opponent with the contradiction between their words and their deeds.
argumentation_figures.example: The safety memo went out on the second. The overtime authorization, waiving the crew rest rule, went out on the third.
argumentation_figures.effect: Lets the opponent's own record perform the refutation.

argumentation_figures.name: categoria
argumentation_figures.definition: Openly accusing an opponent of wrongdoing, to their face and in plain terms.
argumentation_figures.example: You knew the tank was leaking in March, and you approved the sale in April.
argumentation_figures.effect: Ends indirection; the argument becomes a charge that must be answered.
argumentation_figures.caution: Requires proof at the standard the reader will apply, not the one you wish they would.

argumentation_figures.name: contrarium
argumentation_figures.definition: Proving a proposition by establishing the falsity or absurdity of its contrary.
argumentation_figures.example: If secrecy protected the public, the safest counties would be the quietest ones. They are the ones with the most litigation.
argumentation_figures.effect: Argues by elimination in a form compact enough to sit in one sentence.

argumentation_figures.name: dirimens copulatio
argumentation_figures.definition: Balancing a statement by immediately adding a contrary one that strengthens rather than weakens it.
argumentation_figures.example: Not only did the inspection never happen; the form recording it was printed a week before the date it bears.
argumentation_figures.effect: Pre-empts the reader's sense that the case has been overstated by supplying the harder fact.

argumentation_figures.name: antisagoge
argumentation_figures.definition: Coupling a promise of reward for one course of action with a threat of punishment for the other.
argumentation_figures.example: Publish the log and the fine stands at what it is. Withhold it and the inquiry becomes a prosecution.
argumentation_figures.effect: Frames a choice as a fork with unequal exits.

argumentation_figures.name: enthymeme
argumentation_figures.definition: A compressed syllogism in which one premise, usually the general one, is left unstated because the audience supplies it.
argumentation_figures.example: He signed without reading; of course the clause survived.
argumentation_figures.effect: Argues at speed by letting the audience carry the premise they already accept.
argumentation_figures.caution: The unstated premise is where the argument hides; state it when the reader might not share it.

argumentation_figures.name: epicheireme
argumentation_figures.definition: An expanded syllogism in which each premise is stated together with the reason supporting it.
argumentation_figures.example: Sites without a resident supervisor fail inspection, because no one is present to stop work; this site had no resident supervisor, because the post was vacant from March; therefore this site was going to fail.
argumentation_figures.effect: Fortifies each step so the conclusion cannot be attacked through a soft premise.
argumentation_figures.caution: Heavy on the page; use where the stakes justify the machinery.

argumentation_figures.name: sorites
argumentation_figures.definition: A chain of linked propositions in which the predicate of each becomes the subject of the next, ending in a conclusion joining the first term to the last.
argumentation_figures.example: Deferred maintenance becomes hidden maintenance; hidden maintenance becomes unbudgeted maintenance; unbudgeted maintenance becomes emergency work; emergency work is what we cannot afford.
argumentation_figures.effect: Carries the reader across a long inference by short, individually acceptable steps.
argumentation_figures.caution: Each link must hold; the form conceals a weak joint better than any other.

argumentation_figures.name: dilemma
argumentation_figures.definition: Presenting an opponent with two alternatives, both of which damage their position.
argumentation_figures.example: Either the report was read, and approved anyway, or it was never read, and the approval was a signature for hire.
argumentation_figures.effect: Closes the exits, so any answer concedes something.
argumentation_figures.caution: Readers look for the third horn; make sure there is not one.

argumentation_figures.name: reductio ad absurdum
argumentation_figures.definition: Refuting a proposition by showing that its consistent application leads to an absurd or unacceptable result.
argumentation_figures.example: If the code is met whenever the paperwork is complete, then a building that has never been visited is compliant until it falls.
argumentation_figures.effect: Destroys a principle by driving it to its terminus rather than contesting it head-on.
argumentation_figures.caution: The absurd conclusion must genuinely follow; a caricature invites the reply that you built it.

argumentation_figures.name: a fortiori
argumentation_figures.definition: Arguing that if a proposition holds in a weaker case, it holds all the more in the stronger one.
argumentation_figures.example: If a warehouse needs an annual inspection, a school built on the same slab needs one more.
argumentation_figures.effect: Extends an accepted judgment to a case the reader has not yet considered.

argumentation_figures.name: elenchus
argumentation_figures.definition: Refutation by cross-examination, drawing an opponent's own answers into contradiction.
argumentation_figures.example: You say the crew was trained. Trained by whom? By the supervisor. And who trained him? The crew.
argumentation_figures.effect: Makes the opponent, not the arguer, produce the refutation.

argumentation_figures.name: exemplum
argumentation_figures.definition: Citing a specific instance, historical or invented, in support of a general claim.
argumentation_figures.example: Consider the pump station at Cross Creek, which failed the same way, for the same reason, in the same decade.
argumentation_figures.effect: Grounds a general claim in something the reader can picture and check.

argumentation_figures.name: paroemia
argumentation_figures.definition: Use of a proverb or common saying to support or summarize a point.
argumentation_figures.example: Cheap roofs, wet books.
argumentation_figures.effect: Borrows the authority of shared experience, which resists rebuttal because it has no author.
argumentation_figures.caution: A proverb ends a paragraph but proves nothing; do not use one where evidence is owed.

argumentation_figures.name: sententia
argumentation_figures.definition: A general moral or practical maxim inserted to crown a passage.
argumentation_figures.example: Every system protects what it measures, and measures what it is willing to be blamed for.
argumentation_figures.effect: Lifts the particular case into a rule the reader takes away.
argumentation_figures.caution: Aphorism density is a strong tell of machine-smoothed prose; earn one per chapter.

argumentation_figures.name: epigram
argumentation_figures.definition: A terse, pointed statement turning on a witty or paradoxical twist.
argumentation_figures.example: The safest building in the county is the one nobody will insure.
argumentation_figures.effect: Compresses a judgment into a form the reader can repeat.
argumentation_figures.caution: Wit invites distrust in serious argument; one epigram close to the evidence, not a string of them.

argumentation_figures.name: locus communis
argumentation_figures.definition: Amplification of a general theme, virtue, or vice that any audience already accepts, applied to the case at hand.
argumentation_figures.example: There is nothing exotic about negligence. It is ordinary, it is cheap, and it is always somebody's job that week.
argumentation_figures.effect: Connects a particular grievance to a shared moral vocabulary.
argumentation_figures.caution: Commonplaces feel like argument and are not; keep them short and return to the facts.

argumentation_figures.name: aetiologia
argumentation_figures.definition: Stating a claim and immediately giving the cause or reason for it.
argumentation_figures.example: The crews stopped reporting near-misses, because the only consequence of a report was a meeting.
argumentation_figures.effect: Fuses assertion and justification so the reader never holds an unsupported claim.

argumentation_figures.name: apodixis
argumentation_figures.definition: Proving a point by appeal to general experience or common knowledge.
argumentation_figures.example: Anyone who has run a night shift knows what a supervisor who never leaves the trailer is worth.
argumentation_figures.effect: Bypasses citation by invoking what the audience already believes.
argumentation_figures.caution: In nonfiction, common knowledge is often a claim in disguise; check whether it needs a source.

argumentation_figures.name: martyria
argumentation_figures.definition: Confirming a claim from one's own experience as witness.
argumentation_figures.example: I stood in that yard in February and counted the tarps.
argumentation_figures.effect: Stakes the writer's credibility directly on the fact.

argumentation_figures.name: apomnemonysis
argumentation_figures.definition: Quoting an approved authority from memory in support of a point.
argumentation_figures.example: The old district engineer used to say that a schedule is a promise made by people who will not be there to keep it.
argumentation_figures.effect: Adds a second voice with standing, without the apparatus of formal citation.
argumentation_figures.caution: Recalled quotation is where misattribution breeds; verify before you print it.

argumentation_figures.name: anamnesis
argumentation_figures.definition: Recalling to mind ideas, events, or persons of the past as evidence or as reproach.
argumentation_figures.example: We have been here before: the same ordinance was drafted in 1994, and withdrawn for the same reason.
argumentation_figures.effect: Puts the present case into a record the audience had forgotten it was part of.

argumentation_figures.name: dicaeologia
argumentation_figures.definition: Defending oneself briefly by giving a plain reason for what was done.
argumentation_figures.example: I published the memo because I had asked for it in writing three times and been told it did not exist.
argumentation_figures.effect: Answers a charge in one economical sentence, which reads as confidence rather than defense.

argumentation_figures.name: proecthesis
argumentation_figures.definition: Defending what one has said or done by setting out the fuller reasoning behind it.
argumentation_figures.example: I named the firm because unnamed defendants teach the next town nothing, and because the record is public.
argumentation_figures.effect: Converts an apparent lapse of judgment into a considered choice.

argumentation_figures.name: anangeon
argumentation_figures.definition: Pleading necessity as the reason for an action that would otherwise be indefensible.
argumentation_figures.example: They ran the line hot because the alternative was to send four hundred people home with no wage that month.
argumentation_figures.effect: Shifts the argument from whether the act was wrong to whether the situation left an alternative.
argumentation_figures.caution: Necessity is the most abused defense there is; test whether the alternatives were really closed.

argumentation_figures.name: asphalia
argumentation_figures.definition: Offering oneself as surety for a promise or a claim.
argumentation_figures.example: If a single figure in the appendix is wrong, take the whole chapter with it.
argumentation_figures.effect: Puts the writer's own standing behind the claim as collateral.

argumentation_figures.name: medela
