argumentation_figures.definition: Excusing or mitigating the fault of a friend or ally that cannot be denied.
argumentation_figures.example: He signed it, and he should not have. He also signed it at two in the morning at the end of a fourteen-day stretch nobody should have worked.
argumentation_figures.effect: Concedes the fact and contests the weight, which is often the only honest defense available.

argumentation_figures.name: restrictio
argumentation_figures.definition: Making an exception to or qualifying a statement just made.
argumentation_figures.example: No one in the office read the report, with the exception of the one person who was later dismissed.
argumentation_figures.effect: Keeps a sweeping claim honest, and the exception usually carries more force than the rule.

argumentation_figures.name: amphidiorthosis
argumentation_figures.definition: Moderating a harsh statement after the fact, once it has already had its effect.
argumentation_figures.example: It was a lie. Or rather it was what people say when they have decided not to find out.
argumentation_figures.effect: Lets the writer strike hard and then appear scrupulous without withdrawing the blow.

argumentation_figures.name: prodiorthosis
argumentation_figures.definition: Preparing the audience in advance for something shocking or offensive that is about to be said.
argumentation_figures.example: What follows is the part of the transcript the family asked me not to print, and I am printing it, with their reasons.
argumentation_figures.effect: Buys permission for the hard passage and signals that the writer knows its cost.

argumentation_figures.name: apagoresis
argumentation_figures.definition: Dissuading from a course of action by setting out the consequences that will follow it.
argumentation_figures.example: Approve the variance and you will spend the next decade defending every variance anyone asks for.
argumentation_figures.effect: Argues forward in time, converting a present decision into a visible future.

argumentation_figures.name: assumptio
argumentation_figures.definition: Introducing a point that will be needed later, before its relevance is apparent.
argumentation_figures.example: Keep in mind that the fiscal year ends in June. It will matter in three chapters.
argumentation_figures.effect: Plants a premise so that the later inference arrives already furnished.

argumentation_figures.name: anacephalaeosis
argumentation_figures.definition: Summary restatement of the principal points already made.
argumentation_figures.example: So: no permit, no inspection, no supervisor, and a signature dated before the visit.
argumentation_figures.effect: Consolidates a scattered case into something the reader can carry away whole.

argumentation_figures.name: metabasis
argumentation_figures.definition: A brief statement of what has been said and what will follow, used as a transition.
argumentation_figures.example: That is how the permit was issued. How it was renewed twice without a visit is the harder story.
argumentation_figures.effect: Keeps the reader oriented across a structural seam.
argumentation_figures.caution: Signposting every section produces a tour-guide voice; use it at real joints only.

argumentation_figures.name: digressio
argumentation_figures.definition: A deliberate departure from the main line of the discourse, followed by a return to it.
argumentation_figures.example: A word here about how counties fund inspectors, because the arithmetic explains everything that follows.
argumentation_figures.effect: Supplies context the argument needs without pretending it was always on the path.
argumentation_figures.caution: Announce the return or the reader will not follow you back.

argumentation_figures.name: apoplanesis
argumentation_figures.definition: Evading the point at issue by leading the discussion to a different one.
argumentation_figures.example: Asked about the missing inspections, the spokesman spoke for six minutes about the county's award for digital record-keeping.
argumentation_figures.effect: As a described move it exposes evasion; as a practiced one it is a fault.
argumentation_figures.caution: Report it; do not perform it. A reader who notices never trusts the argument again.

argumentation_figures.name: diallage
argumentation_figures.definition: Bringing several separate arguments to bear on a single point.
argumentation_figures.example: The engineering, the timeline, the insurer's own file, and the foreman's testimony all converge on the same afternoon.
argumentation_figures.effect: Makes a conclusion look overdetermined, which is harder to dislodge than one strong proof.

argumentation_figures.name: diatyposis
argumentation_figures.definition: Recommending a course of action, often by setting out in detail what following it would look like.
argumentation_figures.example: Publish every permit on the day it issues. One page, one database, no request needed.
argumentation_figures.effect: Converts criticism into a proposal the reader can picture being adopted.

argumentation_figures.name: epicrisis
argumentation_figures.definition: Quoting a passage and then commenting on it.
argumentation_figures.example: The memo says the risk was accepted. Accepted by whom, and on whose behalf, it does not say.
argumentation_figures.effect: Lets the source speak and then be examined, which reads as scrupulous rather than assertive.

argumentation_figures.name: proclees
argumentation_figures.definition: Daring an opponent to do or prove something, in the confidence that they cannot.
argumentation_figures.example: Produce the inspection sheet for that quarter. Any inspection sheet, from any quarter.
argumentation_figures.effect: Converts your burden into theirs in one sentence.
argumentation_figures.caution: Fatal if they can meet it; never issue a challenge you have not already tried to meet yourself.

argumentation_figures.name: paradiegesis
argumentation_figures.definition: Using a short narrative as the way into a point, so the story does the work of an introduction.
argumentation_figures.example: In 1961 a clerk in the same office kept a rain log in a school notebook. That notebook is why we know what happened next.
argumentation_figures.effect: Earns attention before making a claim, and supplies the terms the claim will use.
argumentation_figures.caution: A narrative opening that the argument never touches again is a hook, not a premise.

argumentation_figures.name: retorsion
argumentation_figures.definition: Turning an opponent's own argument or principle back against their position.
argumentation_figures.example: If a rule that is inconvenient may be waived, then the rule they now invoke against us may be waived too.
argumentation_figures.effect: Costs nothing to build, since the opponent supplied the material.
argumentation_figures.caution: Distinct from counter-accusation: retorsion uses their premise, not their sins.

argumentation_figures.name: argument from silence
argumentation_figures.definition: Inferring a conclusion from the absence of a record or a statement where one would be expected.
argumentation_figures.example: Every other inspection that decade produced a memo. For this one there is nothing, and the filing clerk was meticulous.
argumentation_figures.effect: Makes a gap into evidence, which is sometimes the only evidence available.
argumentation_figures.register: formal; history, investigative journalism, legal argument
argumentation_figures.caution: Valid only when you have shown that the record would exist if the event had; otherwise it is a fallacy with footnotes.

argumentation_figures.name: argumentum ex concessis
argumentation_figures.definition: Arguing entirely from premises the opponent has already granted, without asserting anything of your own.
argumentation_figures.example: Take their three admissions and nothing else: the gauge was theirs, the reading was low, and low readings were to be reported.
argumentation_figures.effect: Makes the conclusion unrefusable without retracting something already said in public.
argumentation_figures.caution: Requires an exact record of what was conceded; paraphrasing the concession forfeits the move.

argumentation_figures.name: apologia
argumentation_figures.definition: A formal, reasoned defense of one's own conduct, position, or life, offered as argument rather than apology.
argumentation_figures.example: I have been asked why I signed it. I signed it because the alternative on the table that week was worse, and I will set out both.
argumentation_figures.effect: Converts a defendant into an advocate and moves the exchange onto reasons.
argumentation_figures.caution: The self-justifying structure is visible to readers; concede the strongest charge early or the whole thing reads as evasion.

argumentation_figures.name: chreia
argumentation_figures.definition: A brief anecdote attributed to a named person, ending in the saying or act that makes the point.
argumentation_figures.example: Asked why he kept a rain log by hand, the clerk said the county's gauge had never once been wrong on paper.
argumentation_figures.effect: Fuses evidence, authority, and aphorism into three lines.
argumentation_figures.caution: Chreiai travel and mutate; verify the attribution or attribute it to no one.

argumentation_figures.name: a contrario
argumentation_figures.definition: Arguing from the opposite: if the rule holds in the stated case, the contrary holds in the contrary case.
argumentation_figures.example: The code names three structures that require annual inspection. It follows that the rest do not, which is why nobody looked at this one.
argumentation_figures.effect: Extracts a second, unstated rule from an enumerated one.
argumentation_figures.caution: Only sound when the enumeration was meant to be exhaustive; that is exactly what is usually in dispute.

argumentation_figures.name: a pari
argumentation_figures.definition: Arguing that like cases must be treated alike, so a ruling in one governs the other.
argumentation_figures.example: The same office required a study for a smaller culvert two miles upstream. Parity requires one here.
argumentation_figures.effect: Puts consistency at stake, which institutions defend more reliably than they defend outcomes.
argumentation_figures.register: formal; legal and administrative argument, ethics
argumentation_figures.caution: Invites a search for a distinguishing feature; anticipate the distinction and close it first.

argumentation_figures.name: anaskeue
argumentation_figures.definition: Systematic refutation of a narrative by testing it for obscurity, implausibility, impossibility, inconsistency, impropriety, and inexpediency.
argumentation_figures.example: Take the official account point by point: unclear on the hour, implausible on the rainfall, and inconsistent with its own map.
argumentation_figures.effect: Gives refutation a checklist, so nothing in the opposing story is left standing by accident.
argumentation_figures.register: formal; classical exercise, argument, investigative writing
argumentation_figures.caution: Mechanical when the whole list is run; use the two heads that actually bite.

argumentation_figures.name: kataskeue
argumentation_figures.definition: Systematic confirmation of a narrative by the same heads used to refute one — clarity, plausibility, possibility, consistency, propriety, expediency.
argumentation_figures.example: The clerk's account is clear on the hour, matches the rainfall record, and has not changed in forty years of retelling.
argumentation_figures.effect: Builds credibility structurally instead of asserting it.
argumentation_figures.register: formal; classical exercise, argument, historical writing

argumentation_figures.name: conciliatio
argumentation_figures.definition: Taking the opponent's own evidence or argument and using it for your own conclusion.
argumentation_figures.example: They offer the maintenance log to show diligence. Read the log: three entries in nine years, all in the same hand, all in the same week.
argumentation_figures.effect: Removes an exhibit from their case and installs it in yours.
argumentation_figures.caution: Only works if you can read the whole document aloud; selective use of their evidence invites the same treatment of yours.

argumentation_figures.name: escaping between the horns
argumentation_figures.definition: Answering a dilemma by rejecting its disjunction and showing that a third option was available.
argumentation_figures.example: We are told the county could either fund the study or fund the repair. It could have done what four neighboring counties did and asked the state.
argumentation_figures.effect: Destroys a forced choice by supplying the option that was suppressed.
argumentation_figures.caution: The third option must have been genuinely available at the time, not merely conceivable now.

argumentation_figures.name: grasping the horn
argumentation_figures.aka: taking the dilemma by the horns
argumentation_figures.definition: Answering a dilemma by accepting one of its branches and denying that it leads where the opponent says.
argumentation_figures.example: Yes, we chose to defer. Deferral was the right call in a year with no rain and no money, and the record shows why.
argumentation_figures.effect: Refuses the trap by owning the unattractive branch and defending it on the merits.
argumentation_figures.caution: Committing to a branch you cannot actually defend converts a dilemma into a confession.

argumentation_figures.name: instantia
argumentation_figures.definition: Refuting a general claim by producing one case that satisfies its terms and fails its conclusion.
argumentation_figures.example: Every culvert of that class is said to have been inspected. Here is one, in the same class, that has no inspection record at all.
argumentation_figures.effect: Ends a universal claim in a sentence, with no theory required.
argumentation_figures.caution: Expect the claim to be narrowed rather than dropped; be ready with the second instance.

argumentation_figures.name: distinguo
argumentation_figures.definition: Answering an objection by drawing a distinction, granting the claim in one sense and denying it in another.
argumentation_figures.example: Granted, the office had notice — notice that a study existed. It did not have notice of what the study said.
argumentation_figures.effect: Preserves both the concession and the position, and shifts the dispute onto the distinction.
argumentation_figures.register: formal; scholastic and legal argument, philosophy
argumentation_figures.caution: A distinction without a difference is the most conspicuous bad-faith move in argument; be ready to show the difference does work elsewhere too.

emotional_appeal_figures.name: exclamatio
emotional_appeal_figures.definition: An exclamation expressing strong emotion, usually breaking the syntax of the surrounding prose.
emotional_appeal_figures.example: Twelve years! Twelve years of the same recommendation, retyped.
emotional_appeal_figures.effect: Registers feeling directly and gives the reader permission to feel it too.
emotional_appeal_figures.register: formal to neutral; oratory, heightened narration
emotional_appeal_figures.caution: Exclamation is nearly always weaker than the fact that provoked it; earn it or cut it.

emotional_appeal_figures.name: epiphonema
emotional_appeal_figures.definition: An exclamatory summing-up sentence that crowns a passage with its emotional point.
emotional_appeal_figures.example: So much for the safest county in the state.
emotional_appeal_figures.effect: Closes a passage with a verdict the reader has already reached.

emotional_appeal_figures.name: thaumasmus
emotional_appeal_figures.definition: An exclamation of wonder or astonishment.
emotional_appeal_figures.example: That the building stood at all for six years is the only miracle in this record.
emotional_appeal_figures.effect: Marks the limit of the writer's ability to explain, which itself makes a point.

emotional_appeal_figures.name: adynaton
emotional_appeal_figures.definition: Hyperbole expressed as an impossibility, declaring a thing will happen only when the impossible does.
emotional_appeal_figures.example: The county will publish that file when the river runs uphill through the courthouse.
emotional_appeal_figures.effect: Converts flat denial into a picture, which is more memorable and more contemptuous.
emotional_appeal_figures.register: informal to neutral; polemic, folk speech
emotional_appeal_figures.caution: A stock move in invective; a tired adynaton is worse than a plain negative.

emotional_appeal_figures.name: indignatio
emotional_appeal_figures.definition: Language calculated to arouse the audience's indignation against a person or act.
emotional_appeal_figures.example: They budgeted for the funerals before they budgeted for the ladders.
emotional_appeal_figures.effect: Converts a fact into an outrage the reader owns.
emotional_appeal_figures.caution: Sustained indignation exhausts the reader and starts to sound like the writer's problem.

emotional_appeal_figures.name: bdelygma
emotional_appeal_figures.definition: An expression of hatred or abhorrence toward a person, thing, or act.
emotional_appeal_figures.example: There is no word for a memo that counts survivors as a line item, and no reading of it that leaves you clean.
emotional_appeal_figures.effect: Names disgust openly, which either recruits the reader or loses them.
emotional_appeal_figures.caution: Spends credibility fast; one such passage per book, at most.

emotional_appeal_figures.name: conquestio
emotional_appeal_figures.definition: Arousing pity for a person's suffering or misfortune.
emotional_appeal_figures.example: She kept the second job for the insurance, and the insurance is what the settlement is now being used to repay.
emotional_appeal_figures.effect: Puts a human cost where an abstraction was, so the reader cannot round it off.
emotional_appeal_figures.caution: Manufactured pathos is detectable; let the particulars do it and stay out of the way.

emotional_appeal_figures.name: mempsis
emotional_appeal_figures.definition: Complaint of an injury combined with an appeal for help or redress.
emotional_appeal_figures.example: We have written to four offices. We are writing here because there is no fifth.
emotional_appeal_figures.effect: Combines grievance and request, which is harder to ignore than either alone.

emotional_appeal_figures.name: onedismus
emotional_appeal_figures.definition: Reproaching someone for ingratitude or for failing an obligation.
emotional_appeal_figures.example: The town that paid for the road, the spur, and the tax holiday learned of the closure from a press release.
emotional_appeal_figures.effect: Frames a betrayal in terms of a debt, which makes the moral claim concrete.

emotional_appeal_figures.name: deprecatio
emotional_appeal_figures.definition: Asking pardon, or entreating that a punishment or misfortune be averted.
emotional_appeal_figures.example: Whatever is decided about the firm, spare the apprentices who signed nothing.
emotional_appeal_figures.effect: Separates the guilty from the exposed and appeals for mercy on the second.

emotional_appeal_figures.name: deesis
emotional_appeal_figures.definition: Earnest supplication or entreaty, often invoking something sacred to the audience.
emotional_appeal_figures.example: By whatever you owe the people who work under your signature, read the log before you sign again.
emotional_appeal_figures.effect: Pushes the appeal past argument into obligation.
emotional_appeal_figures.caution: Very high pitch; almost always too much for analytic prose.

emotional_appeal_figures.name: optatio
emotional_appeal_figures.definition: Expression of a wish, usually one the speaker knows may not be granted.
emotional_appeal_figures.example: May the next inquiry be given the subpoena power this one was refused.
emotional_appeal_figures.effect: States the desired outcome without claiming to be able to produce it.

emotional_appeal_figures.name: ara
emotional_appeal_figures.definition: A curse or invocation of evil upon a person or thing.
emotional_appeal_figures.example: Let the plaque outlast the company and be read by everyone who tries the same thing here.
emotional_appeal_figures.effect: Discharges anger in a formal shape, which is older and colder than mere abuse.
emotional_appeal_figures.caution: Archaic in modern nonfiction; usually reads as theater.

emotional_appeal_figures.name: orcos
emotional_appeal_figures.definition: A solemn oath or sworn affirmation of the truth of what is said.
emotional_appeal_figures.example: On the record and under my own name: I saw the second set of books.
emotional_appeal_figures.effect: Stakes the speaker's standing on the claim in the most formal terms available.

emotional_appeal_figures.name: ominatio
emotional_appeal_figures.definition: A prophecy or foreboding of evil to come.
emotional_appeal_figures.example: There are nine more slabs poured to that specification, and eight of them are under schools.
emotional_appeal_figures.effect: Extends the harm into the future, which converts a past failure into a live danger.
emotional_appeal_figures.caution: A prediction in nonfiction is a claim; be prepared to defend the mechanism.

emotional_appeal_figures.name: cataplexis
emotional_appeal_figures.definition: Threatening disaster, punishment, or ruin as the consequence of a course of action.
emotional_appeal_figures.example: Renew that permit and the next inquiry will be held in a criminal court.
emotional_appeal_figures.effect: Applies pressure by making the cost of continuing explicit.

emotional_appeal_figures.name: apocarteresis
emotional_appeal_figures.definition: Casting off all hope in one quarter and turning deliberately to another.
emotional_appeal_figures.example: The board will not act. The board has never acted. This is addressed to the insurers.
emotional_appeal_figures.effect: Dramatizes a change of audience and, with it, a change of strategy.

emotional_appeal_figures.name: eustathia
emotional_appeal_figures.definition: A promise of constancy or steadfastness.
emotional_appeal_figures.example: Whatever the settlement says, the archive stays open and the names stay printed.
emotional_appeal_figures.effect: Answers a threat with commitment rather than argument.

emotional_appeal_figures.name: paenismus
emotional_appeal_figures.definition: An expression of joy or celebration.
emotional_appeal_figures.example: The ladders came in October, all four of them, on a truck everyone went out to watch.
emotional_appeal_figures.effect: Marks relief and, placed after long grievance, measures how small the victory was.

emotional_appeal_figures.name: eucharistia
emotional_appeal_figures.definition: Formal expression of thanks, usually specifying the benefit received.
emotional_appeal_figures.example: Two clerks copied nine hundred pages after hours for a stranger with no standing. This book exists because of that.
emotional_appeal_figures.effect: Discharges an obligation publicly and models the conduct the writer values.

emotional_appeal_figures.name: eulogia
emotional_appeal_figures.definition: Pronouncing a blessing or commendation upon a person or thing.
emotional_appeal_figures.example: Good luck to the small firms that answered the survey honestly; they have the most to lose by it.
emotional_appeal_figures.effect: Confers approval with a formality that marks the writer's own commitments.

emotional_appeal_figures.name: encomium
emotional_appeal_figures.definition: Formal praise of a person, thing, or quality, setting out what deserves admiration and why.
emotional_appeal_figures.example: For thirty years she filed the same objection, in the same three paragraphs, and every one of them proved right.
emotional_appeal_figures.effect: Establishes a standard of conduct in the person of someone who met it.
emotional_appeal_figures.caution: Unqualified praise reads as advocacy; a real encomium admits the limits of its subject.

emotional_appeal_figures.name: paramythia
emotional_appeal_figures.definition: Consoling someone in grief or loss.
emotional_appeal_figures.example: Nothing in this chapter changes the count. It may change whether the count is repeated.
emotional_appeal_figures.effect: Acknowledges that argument cannot repair the loss, which is what makes it bearable to read.

emotional_appeal_figures.name: philophronesis
emotional_appeal_figures.definition: Placating an adversary with mild speech, submission, or courtesy.
emotional_appeal_figures.example: The engineers were doing their jobs with the tools and the hours they were given, and this is not about them.
emotional_appeal_figures.effect: Lowers the temperature so the substantive attack can land on the right target.

emotional_appeal_figures.name: protrope
emotional_appeal_figures.definition: Exhortation to action, reinforced by promises of reward or warnings of loss.
emotional_appeal_figures.example: Ask for the log. Ask in writing, ask twice, and keep what you are sent.
emotional_appeal_figures.effect: Converts persuasion into instruction, giving the reader something to do.

emotional_appeal_figures.name: exuscitatio
emotional_appeal_figures.definition: Stirring the audience's emotion by conspicuously displaying one's own.
emotional_appeal_figures.example: I have read this file nine times, and I still cannot get past the sentence where the risk is described as tolerable.
emotional_appeal_figures.effect: Uses the writer's reaction as a model for the reader's.
emotional_appeal_figures.caution: Announcing your feelings is weaker than causing them; use where the writer is genuinely in the story.

emotional_appeal_figures.name: pathopoeia
emotional_appeal_figures.definition: A general stirring of the passions, by whatever means the passage affords.
emotional_appeal_figures.example: Read the times on the last three entries in the log, and then read the time on the call to the fire service.
emotional_appeal_figures.effect: Moves the audience into the emotional state in which the argument will be received.
emotional_appeal_figures.caution: The oldest charge against rhetoric; when the emotion outruns the evidence, the reader turns.

emotional_appeal_figures.name: exouthenismos
emotional_appeal_figures.definition: An expression of open contempt for a person, argument, or thing.
emotional_appeal_figures.example: The plan was four pages, two of them letterhead.
emotional_appeal_figures.effect: Registers a judgment the argument has already earned, in fewer words than the argument took.
emotional_appeal_figures.register: informal to neutral; polemic, satire, dialogue
emotional_appeal_figures.caution: Contempt spends credibility; the reader must already agree, or you have simply been rude.

emotional_appeal_figures.name: paraenesis
emotional_appeal_figures.definition: A warning of impending evil, delivered as counsel rather than as threat.
emotional_appeal_figures.example: The same rain will come again in this decade, and the same culvert is still in the ground.
emotional_appeal_figures.effect: Makes a forecast into an obligation without accusing anyone yet.
emotional_appeal_figures.caution: A warning that does not name the mechanism reads as prophecy, and prophecy ages badly.

emotional_appeal_figures.name: makarismos
emotional_appeal_figures.definition: Pronouncing someone blessed or fortunate, usually in a formal repeated frame.
emotional_appeal_figures.example: Fortunate are the townships that kept their own rain logs, for they were believed.
emotional_appeal_figures.effect: Confers value by declaration and invites the audience to want to be in the named class.
emotional_appeal_figures.caution: Instantly recognizable as scripture pastiche; one use per book, at most.

emotional_appeal_figures.name: psogos
emotional_appeal_figures.definition: A sustained formal denunciation of a person or institution, the mirror image of the encomium.
emotional_appeal_figures.example: Consider the office itself: its habits, its appetites, its forty-year record of choosing the cheaper of two wrong answers.
emotional_appeal_figures.effect: Organizes anger into a structure, which makes it read as judgment rather than temper.
emotional_appeal_figures.caution: Invective against a named private person is actionable in some jurisdictions and unpleasant in all of them.

emotional_appeal_figures.name: threnos
emotional_appeal_figures.definition: A formal lament for the dead or the lost, given as a set piece.
emotional_appeal_figures.example: For the row of houses on Water Street: their gardens, their porches, the numbers still on the curb.
emotional_appeal_figures.effect: Gives grief a shape the reader can enter, and licenses a slowness the surrounding prose could not carry.
emotional_appeal_figures.caution: The one place where restraint outperforms every intensifier available.

emotional_appeal_figures.name: jeremiad
emotional_appeal_figures.definition: A sustained denunciation of present decline measured against a founding standard, usually ending in a call to return to it.
emotional_appeal_figures.example: They built the first levee by subscription in a single summer. We have spent nine years discussing a culvert.
emotional_appeal_figures.effect: Fuses lament, accusation, and exhortation into one long structure with real forward pressure.
emotional_appeal_figures.register: formal; sermon, political oratory, polemical essay
emotional_appeal_figures.caution: Depends on a founding standard the audience shares; without one it is nostalgia with a raised voice.

emotional_appeal_figures.name: ubi sunt
emotional_appeal_figures.definition: The topos of asking where the vanished have gone, in a series of questions with no answer.
emotional_appeal_figures.example: Where is the machine shop? Where is the freight office? Where are the men who could get a pump running in the dark?
emotional_appeal_figures.effect: Produces loss by inventory, and refuses the consolation an answer would give.
emotional_appeal_figures.register: formal; elegy, historical writing, lyric prose
emotional_appeal_figures.caution: One of the oldest moves in European writing and easily heard as such; keep the inventory concrete and local.

emotional_appeal_figures.name: outdoing topos
emotional_appeal_figures.definition: Praise by comparison that declares the subject to surpass the accepted standard of its kind.
emotional_appeal_figures.example: Every county keeps records. This clerk kept a record that a hydrologist could still use sixty years later.
emotional_appeal_figures.effect: Borrows the prestige of the standard and then hands it to the subject.
emotional_appeal_figures.caution: Invites the reader to check the comparison, which is often the last thing the writer wants.

emotional_appeal_figures.name: modesty topos
emotional_appeal_figures.definition: A conventional profession of the writer's own inadequacy to the subject.
emotional_appeal_figures.example: I am not an engineer, and everything technical here has been checked by two who are.
emotional_appeal_figures.effect: Disarms the objection that the writer is out of their depth, and pre-licenses the errors.
emotional_appeal_figures.caution: Conventional to the point of transparency; readers discount it unless it is followed by a specific limit.

emotional_appeal_figures.name: inexpressibility topos
emotional_appeal_figures.definition: Declaring the subject beyond the writer's power to describe, in place of describing it.
emotional_appeal_figures.example: There is no account of that night that gets the sound right, and this one will not either.
emotional_appeal_figures.effect: Registers magnitude by conceding defeat, which can be more persuasive than the attempt.
emotional_appeal_figures.caution: A licence to skip the hard work; earn it by attempting the description first and showing where it fails.

emotional_appeal_figures.name: carpe diem topos
emotional_appeal_figures.definition: Exhortation to act now on the ground that time is short and the occasion will not return.
emotional_appeal_figures.example: The money is appropriated this year. It will not be appropriated next year, and the culvert does not care either way.
emotional_appeal_figures.effect: Converts a general truth about time into pressure on a specific decision.
emotional_appeal_figures.register: neutral to formal; lyric, oratory, advocacy
emotional_appeal_figures.caution: Manufactured urgency is the standard tool of bad advocacy; the deadline has to be real.

vices_and_decorum_figures.name: barbarismus
vices_and_decorum_figures.definition: Use of a word that is foreign, obsolete, or malformed for the context.
vices_and_decorum_figures.example: The committee was requested to unforget the earlier resolution.
vices_and_decorum_figures.effect: Almost always a fault; in dialogue it fixes a speaker's education or origin in one word.

vices_and_decorum_figures.name: solecismus
vices_and_decorum_figures.definition: A breach of grammatical or syntactic convention.
vices_and_decorum_figures.example: Between you and I, the numbers was never checked.
vices_and_decorum_figures.effect: Marks the speaker as much as the sentence; deliberately used, it is characterization.
vices_and_decorum_figures.caution: The reader cannot tell a deliberate solecism from a careless one unless the voice is established.

vices_and_decorum_figures.name: acyrologia
vices_and_decorum_figures.definition: Use of an inexact or wrong word in place of the right one.
vices_and_decorum_figures.example: The report was a fulsome account of their achievements, and they meant it kindly.
vices_and_decorum_figures.effect: Comic when unintentional in a character, damaging when unintentional in the writer.
vices_and_decorum_figures.caution: Check the near-miss words you like the sound of; this is where authority quietly leaks away.

vices_and_decorum_figures.name: amphibologia
vices_and_decorum_figures.definition: Ambiguity arising from grammar or word order rather than from the words themselves.
vices_and_decorum_figures.example: The inspector reported the collapse to the office he had criticized.
vices_and_decorum_figures.effect: Usually a fault; deliberately used, it lets a statement be defended in either sense later.
vices_and_decorum_figures.caution: In factual writing, ambiguity of this kind is read as evasion even when it is only carelessness.

vices_and_decorum_figures.name: cacemphaton
vices_and_decorum_figures.definition: An ill-sounding or unintentionally lewd combination of words.
vices_and_decorum_figures.example: The board members had a long and vigorous session with the assessors.
vices_and_decorum_figures.effect: Derails a serious sentence into a joke the writer did not make.
vices_and_decorum_figures.caution: Read aloud; this fault is invisible on the page and unmissable in the ear.

vices_and_decorum_figures.name: cacosyntheton
vices_and_decorum_figures.definition: Awkward or ill-formed word order.
vices_and_decorum_figures.example: The county, of the three failures reported, of which two were structural, accepted responsibility for none.
vices_and_decorum_figures.effect: Slows and confuses; a reliable symptom of a sentence revised too many times.

vices_and_decorum_figures.name: cacozelia
vices_and_decorum_figures.definition: Affected style, straining after ornament, learned words, or novelty.
vices_and_decorum_figures.example: The interlocutory ambience of the committee's deliberative praxis remained fundamentally opaque.
vices_and_decorum_figures.effect: Signals that the writer is performing competence rather than exercising it.
vices_and_decorum_figures.caution: The commonest fault in ambitious drafts, and the easiest for a reader to detect.

vices_and_decorum_figures.name: soraismus
vices_and_decorum_figures.definition: Mingling of languages, affectedly importing foreign words where native ones exist.
vices_and_decorum_figures.example: The Gestalt of the project was, faute de mieux, a certain je ne sais quoi of managed decline.
vices_and_decorum_figures.effect: Reads as showing off unless the borrowed term genuinely has no English equivalent.

vices_and_decorum_figures.name: bomphiologia
vices_and_decorum_figures.definition: Bombast: language inflated far beyond the dignity of its subject.
vices_and_decorum_figures.example: The reordering of the stationery cupboard was, he told the meeting, a watershed in the department's history.
vices_and_decorum_figures.effect: Deflates the speaker in the act of inflating the subject.

vices_and_decorum_figures.name: periergia
vices_and_decorum_figures.definition: Overlabored style: excessive ornament expended on a trivial matter.
vices_and_decorum_figures.example: Three paragraphs on the grain of the table at which the decision was not taken.
vices_and_decorum_figures.effect: Distracts from the point and betrays the writer's affection for their own sentences.
vices_and_decorum_figures.caution: The passages you are proudest of are the likeliest specimens; test them against the argument.

vices_and_decorum_figures.name: macrologia
vices_and_decorum_figures.definition: Long-windedness: using more clauses than the sense requires.
vices_and_decorum_figures.example: It is important to note at this juncture that, in terms of the question of timing, the matter of when the inspection occurred is a relevant consideration.
vices_and_decorum_figures.effect: Buries the claim in throat-clearing.
vices_and_decorum_figures.caution: The most reliable machine-prose signature there is; cut every clause that adds no fact.

vices_and_decorum_figures.name: homiologia
vices_and_decorum_figures.definition: Tedious, undifferentiated style in which every sentence sounds like the last.
vices_and_decorum_figures.example: The report was long. The report was detailed. The report was thorough. The report was ignored.
vices_and_decorum_figures.effect: Flattens attention; used deliberately, it can mimic bureaucratic exhaustion.
vices_and_decorum_figures.caution: The signature failure of unvaried sentence length; measure it rather than trusting your ear.

vices_and_decorum_figures.name: tapinosis
vices_and_decorum_figures.definition: Debasing a thing by naming it with an undignified word.
vices_and_decorum_figures.example: They called the memorial the marker, and then the stone, and finally the thing by the gate.
vices_and_decorum_figures.effect: Diminishes by vocabulary, which can be contempt or, tracked over time, forgetting.

vices_and_decorum_figures.name: aschematiston
vices_and_decorum_figures.definition: The absence of ornament: plain, unfigured style, whether from artlessness or from choice.
vices_and_decorum_figures.example: The wall fell at 4:10. Two men were under it. The permit had expired in March.
vices_and_decorum_figures.effect: Strips the prose to fact, which after heavy figuration reads as the most serious voice in the book.
vices_and_decorum_figures.caution: As a fault it is monotony; as a choice it is the strongest contrast available to a figured style.

vices_and_decorum_figures.name: perissologia
vices_and_decorum_figures.definition: Superfluity of words: saying with several what one word already said.
vices_and_decorum_figures.example: He nodded his head in agreement in the affirmative.
vices_and_decorum_figures.effect: Almost always a fault; in dialogue it can mark a speaker filling time.
vices_and_decorum_figures.caution: Distinct from macrologia: this is local redundancy, not long-windedness across a passage.

vices_and_decorum_figures.name: battologia
vices_and_decorum_figures.definition: Futile repetition of the same word or idea, from a speaker who cannot get past it.
vices_and_decorum_figures.example: The point is, the point is, the point I am making is that the point was raised.
vices_and_decorum_figures.effect: As characterization it renders panic or drunkenness exactly; as writing it is dead weight.
vices_and_decorum_figures.caution: Transcripts are full of it; quoting it verbatim can read as mockery of the speaker.

vices_and_decorum_figures.name: hypercorrection
vices_and_decorum_figures.definition: Applying a supposed rule where it does not belong, in the attempt to sound correct.
vices_and_decorum_figures.example: The commissioner thanked the engineer and I for whom the study had been prepared.
vices_and_decorum_figures.effect: Marks anxiety about status more precisely than any description of it could.
vices_and_decorum_figures.caution: In the writer's own voice it undoes the authority the sentence was reaching for.

vices_and_decorum_figures.name: euphuism
vices_and_decorum_figures.definition: An ornate manner built on relentless antithesis, balanced clauses, alliteration, and far-fetched similes from natural history.
vices_and_decorum_figures.example: As the mole mines where it cannot see, so the office moved where it would not look.
vices_and_decorum_figures.effect: Displays a whole education per sentence, and buries the content under the display.
vices_and_decorum_figures.caution: The named historical case of style eating substance; useful now chiefly as a warning and a period effect.

vices_and_decorum_figures.name: gongorism
vices_and_decorum_figures.definition: A deliberately difficult manner of dense Latinate diction, inverted syntax, and learned allusion.
vices_and_decorum_figures.example: The pluvial insufficiencies of that annum the fiscal instrument nowise contemplated.
vices_and_decorum_figures.effect: Makes difficulty itself the aesthetic, which rewards the initiated and excludes everyone else.
vices_and_decorum_figures.caution: Modern readers do not read obscurity as depth; they read it as unwillingness to be checked.

vices_and_decorum_figures.name: aureation
vices_and_decorum_figures.definition: Studding plain prose with polysyllabic Latinate coinages for the sake of elevation.
vices_and_decorum_figures.example: The aqueous superabundance eventuated in the inundation of the scholastic edifice.
vices_and_decorum_figures.effect: Elevates the surface and drains the sense; the reader learns nothing the plain sentence would not have told them.
vices_and_decorum_figures.caution: Alive and well in institutional writing, where it is usually a way of not naming who did what.

vices_and_decorum_figures.name: inkhorn term
vices_and_decorum_figures.definition: A learned borrowing imported into English where a plain word already exists.
vices_and_decorum_figures.example: The office wrote that the culvert had been obtestated, meaning somebody had complained about it.
vices_and_decorum_figures.effect: Signals learning at the cost of communication, and dates the writer to the decade of the borrowing.
vices_and_decorum_figures.register: formal; scholarly and bureaucratic prose, satire
vices_and_decorum_figures.caution: Some inkhorn terms won and are now ordinary; the test is whether the plain word does the job.

vices_and_decorum_figures.name: purple prose
vices_and_decorum_figures.definition: Passages of ornate, intensified writing conspicuously out of proportion to their occasion.
vices_and_decorum_figures.example: The rain, that ancient and pitiless arbiter of the fates of small towns, descended upon the sleeping valley.
vices_and_decorum_figures.effect: Announces the writer's emotion instead of producing the reader's.
vices_and_decorum_figures.register: neutral; the standing fault of description
vices_and_decorum_figures.caution: It clusters at the ends of chapters and around the deaths of characters; check those places first.

vices_and_decorum_figures.name: cliche
vices_and_decorum_figures.definition: A phrase or figure so worn by use that it is read as a unit and processed without attention.
vices_and_decorum_figures.example: At the end of the day, the perfect storm of factors meant the county was between a rock and a hard place.
vices_and_decorum_figures.effect: Costs nothing to write and returns nothing to the reader, who has stopped seeing the words.
vices_and_decorum_figures.caution: The default output of any writer working fast, human or otherwise; it is the first thing a revision pass should hunt.

vices_and_decorum_figures.name: elegant variation
vices_and_decorum_figures.definition: Reaching for a synonym solely to avoid repeating a word, so that a single referent acquires several names.
vices_and_decorum_figures.example: The culvert failed in June. The drainage structure had been inspected in May, and the concrete conduit was replaced in September.
vices_and_decorum_figures.effect: Buys a small acoustic relief at the price of making the reader check whether three things or one are being discussed.
vices_and_decorum_figures.caution: Repeat the noun. In technical and legal prose, repetition of the exact term is a duty, not a lapse.

vices_and_decorum_figures.name: noun pile
vices_and_decorum_figures.definition: A string of stacked nouns used as modifiers, leaving the reader to guess at the grammatical relations.
vices_and_decorum_figures.example: County culvert failure study funding deferral memo.
vices_and_decorum_figures.effect: Saves four words and costs the reader two readings.
vices_and_decorum_figures.register: neutral; headlines, technical and bureaucratic writing
vices_and_decorum_figures.caution: Three nouns is the practical limit; past that, unpack it with prepositions.

vices_and_decorum_figures.name: circular definition
vices_and_decorum_figures.definition: A definition that uses the term being defined, or a mere synonym of it, in the definition itself.
vices_and_decorum_figures.example: An adequate structure is one whose capacity is adequate to the flow it is required to carry.
vices_and_decorum_figures.effect: Looks like a definition and settles nothing, which is occasionally the intent.
vices_and_decorum_figures.caution: Common in regulations, where it usually marks a question the drafters could not agree on.

vices_and_decorum_figures.name: dangling modifier
vices_and_decorum_figures.definition: A modifying phrase whose implied subject is absent from or different from the subject of the clause it attaches to.
vices_and_decorum_figures.example: Having sat in a drawer for six years, the commissioner finally read the study.
vices_and_decorum_figures.effect: Attaches an action to the wrong actor, usually with unintended comedy.
vices_and_decorum_figures.register: neutral; the standing fault of participial openings
vices_and_decorum_figures.caution: It multiplies in prose that front-loads participles for rhythm; check every sentence that opens with an -ing phrase.

vices_and_decorum_figures.name: malaphor
vices_and_decorum_figures.definition: The blending of two fixed idioms into one that belongs to neither.
vices_and_decorum_figures.example: We will burn that bridge when we come to it.
vices_and_decorum_figures.effect: Funny when a character does it, and an accidental confession of inattention when a writer does.
vices_and_decorum_figures.caution: Distinct from mixed metaphor: this is two frozen phrases colliding, not two live images.

vices_and_decorum_figures.name: sesquipedalianism
vices_and_decorum_figures.definition: The habit of choosing long words where short ones would serve.
vices_and_decorum_figures.example: The precipitation event necessitated the utilization of supplementary pumping capacity.
vices_and_decorum_figures.effect: Slows reading, flattens rhythm, and reads as an attempt to sound authoritative rather than to be understood.
vices_and_decorum_figures.caution: Some long words are the exact words; the fault is reaching for length, not using a precise term.

vices_and_decorum_figures.name: anachronism
vices_and_decorum_figures.definition: Placing a word, object, attitude, or institution outside the period it belongs to.
vices_and_decorum_figures.example: A 1958 county engineer described as pushing back on the timeline.
vices_and_decorum_figures.effect: Breaks the historical frame in one word, and puts every other detail under suspicion.
vices_and_decorum_figures.caution: Vocabulary anachronism is far commoner than object anachronism, and far harder to catch; date the idiom, not just the thing.
